items.title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee
items.summary: ‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains. On Tuesday £10m was released : not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
items.body:
In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains.
On Tuesday £10m was released: not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “restructuring” distressed companies. Under pressure, it extended the deadline by 10 working days before putting this profitable business into administration. It profits more by closing Poundland down and breaking it up.
The manager, whom I’ll call Jim for anonymity, is at work an hour and a half after his paid shift ended. “I look out for my team,” he says, though Gordon Brothers doesn’t seem to be looking out for him. He says the outsourced security staff vanished this week as their pay was stopped. “The shoplifting is very bad now. Look, the high-end stuff has gone first”: the well-known brands, not unknown cheaper makes. Despite everything, he is remarkably proud of the shop and boasts of how much cheaper brands are than in Sainsbury’s. He pats the shelf with red velvet Santa stockings and glittery bows, glad some Christmas stock is in before the closure. “But no one is telling us anything.”
Will the staff get jobs if it closes? He introduces me to a man in his late 50s with an easy manner and a wide grin. “My best man, by far,” he says. “He’s been here 15 years, and never a single day off sick, not one. Will any other shop see how good he is? No, because his English is bad and they won’t know his worth to any manager. I don’t know what he’ll do. I keep putting him on the till to try to improve his English, to help him along.” Jim is proud of his eye for picking good staff and keeping them on warm terms, and is fearful for their future.
This is may not be the sort of shop where you expect steadfast dedication to the company. Jim’s attitude is just another reminder of what I often find reporting on work, that most people are attached to their jobs, despite recent British Social Attitudes research reporting their frustrations. Often the greatest aggravations are about lack of control. Jim says he could increase sales if he was allowed to be the buyer. “I know our customers in this area; the centre doesn’t.”
He belongs to Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, but says there’s nothing it can do. Time and again the union has watched helplessly as these private equity and venture capital buyouts bring down viable retailers. As we talk, a customer asks indignantly why there are no packs of Boost in the cold drinks cabinet. Jim explains the situation and the man looks shocked. “No! You can’t close down! I’m always in here.”
Our surroundings, our streetscape is at the mercy of distant forces. Gap-toothed high streets and boarded-up shops cause us all an ache of loss. Poundland stores teetering on the edge are “anchor stores” drawing people to high streets, but may join those great voids just weeks before Christmas. Woolworths’ 807 stores closed after being taken over, losing 27,000 jobs and lifetimes of local history. BHS, sold for £1, is gone. Debenhams, WHSmith, Toys R Us, Maplin, TM Lewin and plenty more, adversely transformed or taken over by private equity for unkindly “restructure” that usually ends in closures. Some, bought with debts that are loaded on to their balance sheets, stagger but survive – think Asda and Morrisons.
Now it’s Poundland’s turn. At Wednesday’s closed-session select committee on business and trade, MPs heard its long-serving managing director, Barry Williams, challenge the owners, trying to save the business and showing that it made a £18.1m operating profit in the year to September. But Gordon Brothers has turned down offers, notably one from Martin Property Group, owners of NCP car parks.
Through complex financing, it would make more by breaking Poundland up. It has £30m debt to recover but, as it is both the owner and the creditor, it comes top of the list for repayment in administration: after paying tax, it gets paid before any staff who are owed wages. If there’s no money left, redundancy is paid by the taxpayer.
Andy Burnham weighed in demanding answers, but Gordon Brothers has no legal obligation to worry about staff, let alone social or public concerns. The chair of the Commons business and trade committee, Liam Byrne, is campaigning hard to save Poundland, calling Gordon Brothers “much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British high street”, and adding: “It’s clear that they’ve taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife-edge.”
But there’s nothing anyone can do if pressure and shame fails. Why should a company, especially a foreign one, care what anyone thinks when the bottom line says close it down?
Byrne is campaigning to prevent this in future, calling for changes to company law that at present gives shareholders primacy above all else, unlike the much preferable situation in Germany. He would stop pension funds making it their sole obligation to maximise short-term gains and thus investing ever more in venture capital. He’d also impose stress tests to stop asset strippers overloading a business with debt then taking the lion’s share when it’s broken up.
On the Poundland shop floor, Jim and the rest of his team serve their customers and wait another two weeks to discover their fate. A future change in the law is essential. Maybe it will come. But it will probably be too late for them.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Morrisons rolls out flashing digital shelves - is dynamic pricing coming to supermarkets?
items.summary: Shoppers can search for a specific product via the Morrisons loyalty app's 'product finder tool'. The correct shelf-edge label in the supermarket will then light up.
items.body:
Morrisons rolls out flashing digital shelves - is dynamic pricing coming to supermarkets?
Morrisons has launched flashing electronic shelf labels designed to help shoppers find products faster, amid fears dynamic pricing could soon be introduced in British supermarkets.
Shoppers can search for a specific product via the its More Card loyalty app's 'product finder tool'.
The correct shelf-edge label in the supermarket will then light up.
Supermarkets are working at pace to figure out new ways to get shoppers to increase their spending in stores.
For now, Morrisons' flashing shelves are aimed at guiding shoppers to the right product.
But some are concerned supermarket chains across Britain could eventually introduce dynamic pricing.
Dynamic pricing is where the cost of groceries can change by the minute thanks to computer-controlled digital price labels.
Morrisons says it has partnered with French firm Vusion to 'digitise pricing across its entire supermarket estate using electronic shelf labels to automate price updates and improve pricing accuracy'.
Flashy tech: Morrisons is rolling out flashing electronic shelf labels designed to help shoppers find products faster
Andrew Opie, director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: 'Digital pricing displays are simply a way of updating and checking thousands of prices in a fast and cost-effective way, so they can continue to offer great value for customers.'
Morrisons told This is Money it was aligned to the BRC statement on the topic of dynamic pricing.
In April 2026, the Bank of England warned that more businesses were planning to use 'market-responsive pricing tools', with around a third of companies expected to adopt them.
Dynamic pricing technology is already used on shopping websites like Amazon, but supermarkets such as the Co-op have been trialling it in 700 stores nationwide.
While supermarkets in Britain are not currently using dynamic pricing, many, including Co-op and Morrisons, are shifting towards digital shelf labels, which will, in turn, make price changes quicker to implement.
Taking an example, if dynamic pricing was introduced across British supermarkets, a pack of yoghurts could be £1.10 in the morning and £1.50 in the afternoon.
A bottle of wine could be priced 10 per cent higher on a Friday evening – essentially, supermarkets would use customer spending data in an attempt to price 'dynamically'.
Any move towards dynamic pricing in British supermarkets would prove controversial, given that food is an essential purchase unlike concert tickets or flights.
Advocates of dynamic pricing claim shoppers already benefit when prices fall, and have claimed consumers can limit the impact by choosing where and when they buy.
Clive Black, of Shore Capital, told The Times earlier this year: 'Changing prices is very expensive.
'When Tesco changes prices, it has to replace a piece of plastic or cardboard across thousands of stores.
'The initial drive for these displays is operating efficiency, standardisation and compliance, but the longer-term possibility is dynamic pricing.
'Whether that is in the interest of shoppers or shareholders is a moot point.'
Morrisons previously said it would launch its digital flashing shelf units in September this year.
Morrisons said: 'The app will share the in-store location, ask the customer to confirm if they are in the right aisle, and then the corresponding digital shelf label will flash magenta, making it easier for the customer to spot the exact product they want.'
It added: 'The feature is ideal for navigating high-density product aisles like herbs, spices, or sauces, as well as locating popular seasonal items such as cranberry sauce.'
The new technology, which Morrisons claimed was the first of its kind in a British supermarket, will be live in all 270 Morrisons shops that currently have electronic shelf-edge labels installed before Christmas.
Gordon Macpherson, of Morrisons, said: 'We know that Christmas is one of the busiest times of the year for our customers, and we’re always looking for new ways to make their shopping experience as easy and convenient as possible.
'Our new "shop to light" feature is a great example of how we’re using technology to make a real difference in store, helping our customers find the products they need quickly, whether they’re shopping for their Christmas dinner or just popping in to pick up a few last-minute essentials.'
Marks and Spencer has also been testing the use of 'pick to light' shopping technology in its wine aisles.
In its latest half-year results, Tesco said it had more than 7,500 digital advertising screens across the group, including at Booker and convenience chain One Stop.

items.title: Next extends Costa Coffee partnership for another decade
items.summary: Next will continue working with Costa Coffee until 2036, as it continues to expand its in-store food and drink offering. The agreement will see Costa Coffee continue to operate across Next’s UK retail estate, where it currently has more than 140 locations. The partnership began in 2011 with a single concession and has since grown...
items.body:
Next will continue working with Costa Coffee until 2036, as it continues to expand its in-store food and drink offering.
The agreement will see Costa Coffee continue to operate across Next’s UK retail estate, where it currently has more than 140 locations.
The partnership began in 2011 with a single concession and has since grown into a nationwide network, with further openings and investment planned over the next decade.
In 2026, Costa Coffee opened seven new locations within Next stores, including a 3,000 sq ft site at the retailer’s flagship Bluewater destination. It is the largest Costa Coffee location within the retailer’s estate and among the first to feature the coffee chain’s latest store design.
Costa Coffee has also refurbished 26 existing locations across Next’s stores this year, as both businesses look to improve the customer experience and adapt to changing shopping habits.
The extension until January 2036 provides a long-term commitment for Next as it continues to develop its wider retail proposition, using food and drink concessions to complement its core fashion, home and lifestyle offer.
Tom Falk, head of property at Costa Coffee said: “Next has been a valued partner for many years and we’re delighted to extend our relationship through to 2036. This milestone reflects the strength of our partnership and creates an exciting platform for future growth.
“Together, we’ve grown from a single location to a network of more than 140 stores, adapting to changing consumer needs and investing in great coffee experiences along the way.
“The success of landmark locations such as Bluewater demonstrates what can be achieved when two customer-focused brands work together with a shared ambition. This agreement gives us a fantastic opportunity to build on that momentum in the years ahead.”
The deal underlines the growing role of hospitality within traditional retail environments, as retailers look to give shoppers additional reasons to visit stores and extend their time on site.
The continued presence of Costa Coffee strengthens Next’s in-store food and drink offer, supporting its wider strategy to develop larger destination stores.

Following a series of […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Luxury organic food and lifestyle retailer Daylesford is unveiling its Christmas 2026 film, With Love From the Cotswolds, narrated by acclaimed actor Richard E. Grant.
Produced in-house in collaboration with local filmmaker Freddie Jewson, the film places Daylesford’s people, craftsmanship and organic Cotswolds farm at the heart of its festive storytelling.
Following a series of handwritten invitations delivered across the farm, the film brings together Daylesford’s growers, bakers, cheesemakers and florists for an intimate Christmas gathering in a candlelit polytunnel. Narrated through an original poem written in-house and recorded at the farm by Richard E. Grant, the story celebrates the value of slowing down, thoughtful craftsmanship and human connection during the festive season.
Rather than relying on elaborate sets or large-scale production, the creative team adopted a deliberately understated approach, using natural light, real Daylesford team members and the farm’s existing surroundings to create an authentic, cinematic celebration of Christmas.
The film reflects Daylesford’s wider brand philosophy, highlighting the people, provenance and care behind its products while bringing its seasonal campaign, From the Cotswolds, with Love, to life.

items.title: Poundland owner secures two extra weeks to ensure retail chain’s survival
items.summary: US investment firm Gordon Brothers is ‘taking due care’ to consider if one of three bidders has enough funds Business live – latest updates Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal. The management of Poundland , which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning. Continue reading...
items.body:
Poundland’s owner has said it is “taking due care” to consider if one of three bidders had enough funds to ensure its survival after the troubled budget retail chain secured two more weeks to find a deal.
The management of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors on Thursday morning.
Poundland’s board said it had sought the extra time “with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people”.
It added: “Our stores remain open as usual during this period and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.”
The retail chain’s owner, the US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers since Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.
A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said on Thursday: “We support the board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further 10 working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.
“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.
“We are in discussions with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and we have also received several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business.
“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation. We, the board, and all involved are working to secure a credible plan that delivers certainty, preserves value and protects as many jobs as possible.”
Gordon Brothers confirmed it had provided £85m of financing, understood to be via an asset-backed loan that Poundland has only partially used over the past year.
That financing is in addition to a £30m shareholder loan largely taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the business for a nominal £1 last year.
Gordon Brothers fought back after MPs on Wednesday accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers said it had provided finance for Poundland “when no one else was willing to finance the company – and has contributed substantial efforts to support a turnaround.
“Had we not, the company would have collapsed into insolvency in August 2025. Our efforts have continuously focused on the company’s value and its people, not prioritising one over the other.”

items.title: Poundland secures more time as rescue talks continue
items.summary: Poundland has applied for a second notice of intention (NOI) to appoint administrators after its initial 10-working-day protection period expired on Thursday [12 November 2026]. The extension provides a further 10 working days to secure a buyer and avoid insolvency. The discount retailer, which has been grappling with financial difficulties and restructuring its UK store...
items.body:
Poundland has applied for a second notice of intention (NOI) to appoint administrators after its initial 10-working-day protection period expired on Thursday [12 November 2026].
The extension provides a further 10 working days to secure a buyer and avoid insolvency.
The discount retailer, which has been grappling with financial difficulties and restructuring its UK store estate, is seeking further support to protect its operations and safeguard jobs across its network.
Poundland’s board said funding had been agreed to allow the business to continue trading while negotiations progress. Stores will remain open as usual during the extended period.
The development follows mounting political pressure on owner Gordon Brothers, which acquired Poundland for £1 last year, over its handling of the retailer’s financial position.
Following a private meeting with Parliament’s Business and Trade Committee on Wednesday, its chair Liam Byrne accused Gordon Brothers of taking millions of pounds out of the business while it was financially vulnerable.
Gordon Brothers has denied prioritising its financial returns over the retailer’s future, saying it had provided £85m in new financing to support the business.
The investment firm confirmed it was in discussions with three potential buyers for the entire business, alongside receiving several offers from established high street retailers interested in acquiring significant parts of its estate.
Potential buyers include investment firm Xyra Holdings and Irish business Martin Property Group. Tesco has also reportedly explored acquiring up to 150 stores, while Iceland and Lidl are among retailers understood to have expressed interest in parts of the estate.
Around 600 UK stores and 11,000 jobs remain at risk if a rescue cannot be secured.
If negotiations fail, corporate advisory firm AlixPartners is understood to be lined up to oversee an administration process.
The additional breathing space gives Poundland another opportunity to secure a deal that preserves its store network and workforce, as well as maintaining continuity for suppliers ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

items.title: ‘Workers being left behind’ as government cracks down on retail crime, says policy group
items.summary: Westminster policy group, the Policy Liaison Group on Workplace Wellbeing says employers have an “absolute duty” to provide greater employee protection. It was a conclusion drawn from a Wembley Stadium roundtable during CX Vision Live 2035, which took place on Thursday 5 November. As Respect… This story continues at ‘Workers being left behind’ as government cracks down on retail crime, says policy group Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
It was a conclusion drawn from a Wembley Stadium roundtable during CX Vision Live 2035, which took place on Thursday 5 November.
As Respect Week highlights abuse towards retail workers, leading wellbeing experts called for a rethink on how to protect customer-facing employees.
Key insights included:
- Employees are often left to absorb workplace trauma without adequate recovery support.
- Employers must apply the same design discipline to psychological hazards as they do to physical safety.
- Customer-facing staff should actively co-design workplace policies, tools and training.
- Lower-paid workers are typically trapped between customer hostility at the counter and disciplinary action.
- The discussion took place on 5 November and brought together workplace wellbeing and customer experience leaders from the UK, the US and the Gulf.
According to the British Retail Consortium, retail workers experience approximately 1,600 incidents of violence and abuse every day, more than three times pre-pandemic levels. Despite retailers investing an estimated £5bn in security measures over five years, participants questioned whether enough is being done to protect employees (see roundtable summary for more insights).
The discussion identified three priorities for employers and policymakers:
- Invest in employees, not just security measures
While legislation and security measures help tackle retail crime, participants warned that they often overlook the employees dealing with the aftermath. Workers may be expected to return to work immediately following an abusive encounter, with little opportunity to recover.
Gethin Nadin, chair of the PLG, questioned this imbalance, arguing that “there’s an employee in the middle of this, and they’re not the person that’s being invested in.”
Participants called for greater post-incident care, financial support and staffing arrangements that allow employees time to recover.
- Design workplaces for psychological safety
Employers routinely assess physical hazards, but participants questioned whether psychological risks receive the same attention. The discussion highlighted three priorities: practical skills, appropriate tools and workplace design, including de-escalation training and employee involvement in shaping policies.
As Nadin asked, “If you were to prioritise psychological safety or mental health, how would you change the design of your organisation or the processes that you have in place?”
Employees should have a direct role in identifying risks and developing solutions.
- Stop leaving employees to bear the consequences of corporate decisions
Customer-facing workers often enforce pricing changes and restrictive policies they had no role in developing, leaving them exposed to customer frustration.
One participant described employees as “literally the representation of the decision”. Others highlighted the pressure to enforce policies despite personal safety concerns, describing it as “a choice between do I get fired or attacked?”
Participants called for senior leaders to spend more time in customer-facing roles and involve employees in decisions likely to provoke confrontation.
During the discussion, David Liddle, founder and CEO of The TCM Group, said: “I propose that retailers, trade associations, community safety partnerships, police forces, and restorative practitioners explore a new RISE (Retailers Investing in a Safer Environment) pilot.
“The ambition is clear: equip people to recognise risk, manage conflict safely, prevent harm where possible, and create communities in which everyone feels respected and protected. Safer shops can become a starting point for safer communities.”
Clemens Moehring, COO at Hastee, said: “When a retail worker experiences abuse, security deals with the incident and payroll deals with their pay. But who is looking at the connection between the two?
“Financial insecurity can make it harder for employees to report abuse, take time off to recover or even consider leaving an unsafe working environment. Financial wellbeing needs to be part of how employers prevent and respond to workplace violence.”
The PLG will share its findings with parliamentarians and policymakers, calling for closer collaboration between government, employers and trade unions to protect employees before, during and after incidents of abuse.
Joanne Thomas, general secretary of Usdaw, commented: “Nobody should be afraid to go to work, so it is of grave concern that Usdaw’s latest survey findings show that 12% of retail workers were assaulted last year, with around three-quarters being abused or threatened.
“The government is making a difference with investment in police, but they need to bring into force the protection of shop workers law passed by Parliament in April. Usdaw works closely with retailers to make shops safer.
“Usdaw’s volunteer health and safety reps are regularly risk assessing workplaces and discussing mitigations with managers. We encourage retail employers who don’t currently engage with Usdaw to work with us to help make their workplaces safer.”
The Retail Trust commented: “Our country’s shop workers have had enough of being shouted at, threatened, and treated with contempt.
“We’re hearing from people who are frightened to come into work because they don’t know what they’ll face that day, and from others who have been pushed to breaking point by repeated abuse.
“Retail is one of the few places where millions of strangers still interact face-to-face and there has been a disturbing shift over the last few years where behaviour that would once have been considered completely unacceptable is increasingly being seen as part of the job. This is damaging people’s confidence, destroying morale and driving good people out of a sector they once loved.
“Most people do the right thing, but when a minority don’t, the rest of us have a role to play in making sure shop workers still feel seen and valued.
“No one should face abuse at work and respect can start with something as simple as looking someone in the eye, showing a little patience or simply saying, ‘hello.’”

items.title: Matalan set to open four stores in time for Christmas
items.summary: As Matalan prepares for the peak rush, the fashion retailer is investing in its store network with four openings this November. The openings are in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, and Newport in Wales, as well as Bangor as part of its Northern Ireland investment. They form part of a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores...
items.body:
As Matalan prepares for the peak rush, the fashion retailer is investing in its store network with four openings this November.
The openings are in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, and Newport in Wales, as well as Bangor as part of its Northern Ireland investment.
They form part of a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores and bring its improved shopping experience to more customers.
James Dorling, property director at Matalan, commented: “Our stores play a huge role in how customers experience Matalan, so it’s essential that they reflect the improvements we’re making to our product and brand.
“That’s been the focus of our investment over the past two years – not just making stores look better, but making them easier to shop and better at showcasing what we have to offer. It’s about investing in the right locations, improving the shopping environments, and giving our customers even more reasons to choose Matalan.”
The new locations represent nearly 100,000 sq ft of new retail space and will employ around40 colleagues per store.
Additionally, the sites are designed to showcase the improvements being introduced across Matalan’s wider estate, including brighter interiors, simpler layouts and enhanced visual merchandising. The retailer has also worked to boost its fashion and homeware collections.
Matalan said its store investment has been delivering encouraging results, with the retailer’s Derby store, which opened earlier this year and introduced Matalan’s latest, more modern store format, becoming its most successful opening to date, reaching £1m in sales in just 51 days.
Dorling added: “The response to the changes we’ve made has been really positive, with Derby a particular highlight. The four openings this November mark another important milestone in our investment programme, and we’re delighted to be bringing the latest Matalan experience to more communities in time for Christmas.”

items.body:
Cornish Bakery has secured an eight-figure funding package from its new banking partner, HSBC UK, to support its next phase of growth and investment.
The funding will support expansion and investment in its people, bakeries and customer experience. The business is also spending more than £1.6m on refurbishments this winter, with its new Guildford bakery due to open on 25th November.
The backing follows five years of growth during which Cornish Bakery has doubled its number of bakeries, quadrupled profit and created jobs for 1,000 people. Cornish Bakery reports strong like-for-like sales growth over summer 2026, alongside six new bakery openings.
This year also saw the launch of RISE by Cornish Bakery, its larger-format concept. The first opened in Betws-y-Coed, followed by a two-storey, 3,500 sq. ft. bakery at Gunwharf Quays in Portsmouth, its largest location to date.
As Cornish Bakery continues to expand, protecting the individuality of its people and bakeries remains fundamental to its approach. Rather than pursuing the traditional cookie-cutter model of national expansion, the business is embracing what founder Grocutt describes as an ‘anti-brand strategy’, with each new bakery individually designed and curated to reflect the community it serves.
Mat Finch, managing director of Cornish Bakery, said: “Our next phase is about investing intelligently, finding brilliant locations and building bakeries that belong in their communities. We’re delighted to have HSBC UK’s support which will really help us to maximise our potential.”
Liam Gover, relationship director at HSBC UK, said: “Cornish Bakery has a clear sense of what makes its business distinctive and how it wants to grow. We’re pleased to support investment in its bakeries and new locations while helping it retain the individual character of each site.”
Cornish Bakery has 81 bakeries and a team of more than 1,000. For more information on the company and its bakeries, visit www.thecornishbakery.com.

Houston Hot Chicken (HHC), the cult favourite US chicken brand known for serious heat, queues round the block and openings that feel like a party, is bringing its fire to Watford for its third UK restaurant.
Watford, your chicken game is about to get a serious upgrade. Houston Hot Chicken (HHC) is landing in town with juicy buttermilk-marinated chicken, hand-breaded then dialled up to whatever heat you can handle. Think stacked hot chicken sandwiches, sensational tenders, loaded fries, house-made lemonades and irresistible shakes – you better come hungry.
After debuting in Stevenage in October and with Brunswick Centre next in line, HHC is moving fast to bring its bold American flavours to more UK neighbourhoods as part of the PizzaExpress House of Brands.
Watford’s chicken fans have a new name to add to the must-try list. HHC’s menu is all about the chicken. There are stacked hot chicken sandwiches dripping with sauce, hand-breaded tenders made for dunking, and loaded fries piled high. Add ice-cold house lemonades and thick slurpable shakes and you’ve got everything covered for a quick lunch or full-on feast with friends.
Every order starts with a choice of heat, from a gentle kick all the way up to the top of the scale. That’s where you’ll find “Houston, We Have A Problem” A scorching two million on the Scoville scale. It’s so hot it comes with paperwork… waiver signed, bragging rights secured. If you’re not chasing glory? Every level further down the scale still delivers the big, bold flavour with zero compromises.
Ben Lawrence, International Director at PizzaExpress, said: “Watford, get ready. Houston Hot Chicken is coming to town and we can’t wait for you to try it.
We’re moving quickly. After Stevenage and with Brunswick Centre coming up next, Watford is a big step in taking HHC’s bold flavours and energy to more people across the UK. The momentum is real and this is only the beginning.”
The brand isn’t messing around, and not only is it landing in Watford, for some, it’s coming straight to the door. From Monday 16 November, HHC is also launching its Crouch End delivery kitchen, which will bring the heat to North London through Deliveroo. Whether it’s a Friday night feast, a midweek pick-me-up or the centrepiece of your next mates’ night in, just pick your heat, place your order and let HHC handle dinner.
For those in Watford, the exact opening date and launch-day celebrations will be revealed soon. To be the first to hear follow @HHC_UKI on Instagram and TikTok.
Watford, we have lift-off. Countdown to the first bite starts now.

items.title: Why independent retailers should rethink how they source branded stock
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Independent retailers and online sellers in the UK still buy a lot of branded stock the same way they did a decade ago. They open a trade account with one or two distributors, accept the minimum order, and hope the price they were quoted last month still holds. That model was built for larger multiples. […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Independent retailers and online sellers in the UK still buy a lot of branded stock the same way they did a decade ago. They open a trade account with one or two distributors, accept the minimum order, and hope the price they were quoted last month still holds. That model was built for larger multiples. But for a high-street chemist, a beauty independent or a small online seller, it is an expensive way to keep shelves full.
The squeeze is easiest to see in health, beauty and household lines, where ranges turn over quickly and cash is tighter than it was a few years ago. Buying from EU suppliers can still mean paperwork and unexpected costs at the border. The independents who are coping are not necessarily the ones with the biggest buying power. They are the ones who have changed how they source.
The problems that still get in the way
Minimum order quantities and minimum order values remain the first barrier. Many brand distributors still set thresholds for national retailers. A small shop that wants to test a new skincare line, or refill a bestseller without taking six months of stock, is told the pallet is the smallest unit available. Cash then sits in the stockroom rather than in the business, and a product that does not sell becomes a write-down rather than a lesson.
Distributor gatekeeping is the second problem. Official channels are limited to a short list of authorised partners. Getting an account can mean lengthy onboarding, proof of volume, or a territory already reserved for someone else. Independents are left waiting, or they go without a brand their customers are already asking for. Some turn to unofficial sellers, which creates a different problem: proving the stock is genuine when a customer, or a marketplace such as Amazon, asks for paperwork.
Price swings make planning harder still. A quote agreed in March can look very different by June, especially when goods are priced in euros and sterling moves, or when a supplier revises its list after a shortage. For many buyers, comparing offers remains a manual job: spreadsheets, email attachments and stock lists that are out of date by the time they are opened. And you cannot tell whether you are paying a fair wholesale price when you can only see one offer.
None of this means traditional distributors have no place. For stable, high-volume lines, a long-standing account can still work well. The issue is relying on that route for everything, including the products you only want to try, and the ones where prices move week to week.
What actually works
The more useful shift has been towards B2B wholesale marketplaces. Instead of negotiating a separate account with every supplier, buyers can see offers from many verified wholesalers, brands and distributors in one catalogue, and choose the one that works for that order. That reduces the time spent chasing stock lists, and it makes it harder for a single supplier to set the price unchallenged.
Comparing offers across verified suppliers matters as much as the size of the catalogue. Authenticity is not optional in health, beauty and household. Independents need to know the goods are genuine, and that they will receive the invoices and supply-chain documents required for resale, including on third-party marketplaces. A marketplace that vets its suppliers, and lets you see more than one offer on the same product, gives you both a price check and a clearer chain of supply.
Smaller orders are the other change that should have happened years ago. If the minimum order value is low enough, you can test a line, refill what is selling, and avoid tying up cash in stock you are not sure about. This matters most for independents who cannot justify the minimums still common in traditional wholesale.
Seeing the full landed cost before committing is just as important as the headline unit price. Shipping, duty and VAT can turn an attractive quote into a poor margin once the goods arrive. The better wholesale routes now include shipping in the price, put duties into the quote on EU-UK orders, and handle import VAT so a UK buyer is not left settling extras with a courier at the door.
That is the approach we take at Qogita, a European health and beauty wholesale platform. Buyers compare offers from more than 600 vetted suppliers, covering over 20,000 brands, in a single catalogue, with no contracts and a minimum order value of €500. Goods are sent from supplier warehouses in the EU and the UK. For UK buyers, Qogita handles customs clearance on EU-UK orders, includes the duties in the price, and pays import VAT on their behalf. Shipping, and cover against loss or damage in transit, are included in the price, and the invoices are designed to meet the requirements of third-party marketplaces.
None of that replaces good buying discipline. Retailers still need to know their margins, their rate of sale, and which brands their customers actually want. A longer list of health and beauty wholesale suppliers is only useful if it is used to compare terms, not to fill a basket. But the old assumption, that independents have to accept high minimums, closed distribution and opaque pricing because they are small, no longer holds. The retailers who treat sourcing as a choice, order by order, will be in a stronger position than those still waiting for a single distributor to say yes.

items.title: Burberry returns to profit as sales soar, from £85 socks to £9,000 coats
items.summary: CEO says ‘democratic approach’ has helped brand outperform tough market, with big rises in China and US Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer. Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said. Continue reading...
items.body:
Burberry has returned to profit as its back-to-basics strategy drove strong sales of the British brand’s coats, jackets and handbags over the summer.
Joshua Schulman, the chief executive, said the luxury brand had outperformed a “challenging luxury market” to achieve sales growth of 6%, helped by strong online and wholesale sales particularly in China and the US. “Our strategy is working,” he said.
Burberry said it made a pre-tax profit of £19m in the six months to 26 September after a loss of £48m a year before, as sales rose to £1.1bn. Sales rose 15% in China and 14% in the Americas but fell 1% in the Europe and Middle East region, partly due to the Iran war.
Schulman said Burberry’s focus on a “pyramid of pricing” ranging from more “affordable” scarves, starting from £195, and cotton-cashmere socks from £85, to its top-tier bags and coats, which can cost more than £9,000 for a leather version, had helped it achieve growth despite a tough market. Wealthy shoppers around the world are travelling less and being more cautious about spending, hitting luxury brand sales globally.
Sales of lightweight jackets and “tropical” gaberdine raincoats as well as its Cotswold range of leather bags and accessories featuring the brand’s famous check had proved popular.
Schulman said: “Luxury customers around the world are experiencing some fatigue with exorbitant pricing and in this context our strategy of having great value for money is resonating strongly with Chinese customers.”
“Burberry has always had a somewhat more democratic approach than some of our European peers and has a universal appeal,” he added.
Schulman said the brand had spent the last two years of its Burberry Forward strategy returning to its historical position at the “sweet spot in the luxury market”.
He said investment in locally relevant marketing, such as special product for China’s Valentine’s Day celebrations this spring and for the upcoming lunar new year, were also helping drive sales.
“It is no secret global tourism is down but the local customer has been spending in their respective regions,” Schulman said. “This is a trend we have been seeing all year long.”
While people were spending less as tourists which was hitting sales in discount outlets, Schulman said local spending was holding up in the brand’s flagship city centre stores including in London.
He said that while “nobody has a crystal ball” about whether customers would begin spending more freely, history suggested “this is a very cyclical business”.

items.body:
By Laura McLindon, head of technical – Food and FBH, Fortnum & Mason
For more than 300 years, Fortnum & Mason has built its reputation on exceptional products, from our famous hampers and teas to own-brand food collections. Today, we source products from thousands of suppliers, ranging from global brands to small artisan producers. As a Royal Warrant holder, maintaining the quality and compliance standards expected of our products is fundamental to how we operate.
As the business grows, developing those products has become increasingly complex. More suppliers, more product information, and stricter quality and compliance requirements demand greater coordination before products reach customers.
To support our next phase of growth, Fortnum & Mason has selected Oracle Retail Brand Compliance Management to modernise the way products are developed and managed while maintaining the standards that define our brand.
This technology builds on our Oracle footprint which also includes Oracle Simphony Cloud Point of Sale to manage transactions across many of our restaurants. Together, these technologies support key areas of our business operations as we continue to grow.
Modernising product management at scale
Managing the end-to-end product lifecycle across a supplier network of our size requires close coordination between our teams and suppliers, from initial product specifications and approvals through to compliance and launch.
By implementing Oracle Retail Brand Compliance Management, we’re bringing supplier information, product specifications, approvals, and development workflows together in one place. Instead of manually tracking information across different systems, our teams and suppliers will be able to work from the same up-to-date information.
This will mean less time spent on administration and manual processes, better collaboration with suppliers, and a streamlined path from product idea to launch, giving our teams more time to focus on delivering high quality and innovative products.
Protecting the quality behind every product
Quality and compliance are central to our product development process, particularly when working with such a diverse supplier network. Having greater visibility of product and supplier information will help our teams maintain those standards as the business expands.
With Oracle we will have greater visibility and governance across the product lifecycle, with a connected view of ingredient data, supplier records, compliance documentation, packaging information, and sustainability data to support the high standards we maintain as a Royal Warrant holder. With everything in one place, our teams can make informed decisions, maintain end-to-end product traceability, and respond quickly to supplier or regulatory changes to ensure our customers have a seamless buying experience
Supporting future growth
By bringing supplier, product and compliance information all together on one platform, we’re creating a strong foundation for future innovation, including the ability to take advantage of Oracle’s expanding AI capabilities.
As the retail industry evolves, having connected and reliable information is becoming just as important as the products themselves. With Oracle, we’re giving our teams the tools to manage increasing complexity while continuing to deliver the quality, trust, and experience our customers
To see these technologies in action, join us at the National Retail Federation (NRF) show Booth #5838 in NY, January 10-12.

items.title: Poundland staves off immediate collapse as emergency talks continue
items.summary: A notice to appoint administrators for Poundland expired at midnight, with 600 stores and 10,500 jobs at stake, plus thousands more in the supply chain.
items.body:
Poundland staves off immediate collapse as emergency talks continue
Bosses at Poundland have this morning held a board meeting to determine the firm's future after it secured a two-week reprieve to secure a rescue deal.
A new notice of intention to appoint administrators was filed this morning, giving Poundland 10 days to find a new buyer.
This week, owner Gordon Brothers told a committee of MPs they were in favour of extending the deadline, which was due to expire at midnight.
It represents a last-ditch effort to stave off the discount chain's immediate collapse, and with it Poundland's 600 shops and 10,500 employees.
But Barry Williams, managing director of Poundland, said there were 'no guarantees' jobs would be saved ahead of talks with colleagues.
Mr Williams, who met MPs alongside Gordon Brothers in private on Wednesday, said they were able to 'share some more detail - we left them with some facts.'
Liam Byrne MP, who chairs the business committee, said it had been 'one of the most extraordinary evidence sessions I have ever seen,' accusing the retailer's owners of 'behaving almost like a Wolf of Wall Street, rampaging the British high street.'
In the balance: Bosses at Poundland have held a board meeting to determine the firm's future
Politicians and retail veterans previously warned the demise of the company exposes a worrying trend that has seen private equity vultures prey on household names across Britain.
Poundland has been edging towards administration after Gordon Brothers rejected a rescue bid for Poundland – sparking fears it is trying to sell the group off piecemeal rather than secure its future.
Meanwhile, the private equity firm has also frozen approximately £50million of the retailer's cash, leaving bosses unable to restock shelves.
Gordon Brothers has released around £11million and committed further funds next week to enable the retailer to continue operations.
It has been reported that Gordon Brothers is assessing three offers, including one from the little-known Xyra Group Holdings, to acquire Poundland in its entirety.
But if no rescue deal comes to fruition, the chain and its components would most likely be broken up, with other retailers potentially snapping up batches of shops.
Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor, told This is Money: 'The clear fly in the ointment remains the owners, who seem to be favouring selling the store estate and its stock piecemeal rather than accepting any bids for the business as a whole.
'The clock is ticking quickly and the outcome will be determined by the stance of the owners.
'More broadly, the rebirth of the high street is a tough nut to crack. The pandemic firmly entrenched online shopping as the preferred route for consumers, although Poundland’s value offering would continue to appeal to an increasingly cash-strapped consumer if a rescue can be found.'
Julie Palmer, managing partner at BTG, said: 'A further two weeks of protection, subject to court approval, is good news for Poundland’s staff, suppliers, and customers.
'It gives the credible bidders time to firm up their offers and could yet avoid an administration in the run-up to Christmas.'
She added: 'But time alone won’t save the business. A sale now depends on Poundland having proper access to its cash so it can restock for Christmas, and on the bidders producing funded, deliverable offers.
'The gap between what’s on the table and what’s owed to the shareholders is the sticking point.
'If the owner is prepared to accept a solvent deal rather than hold out for full recovery, as Pepco has signalled it is, the chances of a sale are materially better than they were 24 hours ago. These next two weeks are critical.'
Poundland has been battling against rivals like B&M and Home Bargains, but its performance has improved in the past year.
Steve Smith, Poundland's co-founder, said the retailer looked set to report between £18million and £20million of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation.
Last year, Gordon Brothers purchased Poundland for less than £1.

items.body:
Waitrose is officially opening its brand-new 15,000 sq ft supermarket on The Square in Hale Barns today, bringing its quality food, expert service, and community involvement to thousands more customers in Greater Manchester.
This highly-anticipated opening marks the next phase of Waitrose’s £1 billion nationwide investment plan, to deliver the very best experience for customers across its shops, online offering and partner sites.
The team at Waitrose Hale Barns brings together three experienced Partners who transferred over to the branch and 73 new recruits joining the John Lewis Partnership.
Located in the heart of the village, the new branch is designed as a complete destination for food lovers with more than 15,000 products on offer. Central to the offering is Waitrose’s approach to quality, food integrity and animal welfare. Key features include dedicated meat, fish and sushi counters, dry-aged beef cabinet, hand-cut and speciality cheeses, and a fruit and veg section championing organic, Fairtrade, and regeneratively-farmed produce.
Customers can explore the fully stocked, fresh-in-store bakery and patisserie and curated ranges including Waitrose No. 1, Essential Waitrose, and Waitrose Duchy Organic, alongside an expansive selection of award-winning wines – including a selection of Fine & Rare bottles – and low-and-no alcohol options.
Customer convenience is central to the store, offering Click & Collect services for John Lewis, Waitrose Entertaining and Waitrose Cellar, and rapid home delivery via Deliveroo and UberEats.
My Waitrose members can enjoy a host of benefits including personalised offers, free hot drinks and products and 20% off selected fish counter products every Friday.
The store features Electronic Shelf Labels, freeing up Partners from manual updates and allowing them to dedicate even more time to delivering the outstanding customer service Waitrose is known for. Partners are also equipped with a first-of-its-kind AI app, providing instant advice on product availability, wine pairings, and cooking and recipe recommendations.
As part of its commitment to the area, Waitrose Hale Barns will donate £12,000 annually to local charities and community groups through its Community Matters initiative.
Freddie Sackey-Addo, Waitrose regional manager, said: “After months of hard work behind the scenes, seeing the first shoppers walk through the doors this morning was a huge moment for all of us.
“This destination store has been designed around a genuine passion for food – from our Partners working on the counters and bakery to the curated wine selection and fresh fruit, vegetables and more. We hope our customers treat this as their neighbourhood shop, whether they’re grabbing a quick lunch, looking for advice on what to have for dinner, or discovering something new during their regular weekly shop. Hale Barns is a great location and we can’t wait to meet all our new customers.”
Joining the ribbon-cutting ceremony was Connor Rand, MP for Altrincham and Sale West, who said: “It’s wonderful to see Waitrose investing in this new store in the heart of Hale Barns. It’s a clear demonstration of what a vibrant and welcoming community we have to attract such a big national brand to our high street.
“I know that local residents in Hale are very much looking forward to the opening and I’m sure Waitrose will become a valued part of our community.”
To celebrate the opening, the very first customer through the doors at 8am received a bouquet of flowers. Shoppers were also treated to welcome drinks, food tastings, and free commemorative tote bags.

items.title: Two men jailed for running fraudulent Pontypool store, with illegal products seized
items.summary: Two men have been imprisoned after significant quantities of illicit tobacco, cigarettes and illegal vapes were discovered in a concealed storage area in a Pontypool high street store. Tashin Mokhtar and Arish Mohammedi pleaded guilty to several offences at Newport Crown Court on Friday, including… This story continues at Two men jailed for running fraudulent Pontypool store, with illegal products seized Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Tashin Mokhtar and Arish Mohammedi pleaded guilty to several offences at Newport Crown Court on Friday, including carrying on a fraudulent business.
The court heard Trading Standards officers received information in March 2023 that Pontypool Shop was selling illegal tobacco and disposable vapes which did not meet UK safety standards.
Initial test purchases confirmed the sale of counterfeit cigarettes and hand-rolling tobacco and subsequent inspections found further illegal cigarettes and counterfeit tobacco, and non-compliant disposable vapes.
A search was carried out at the premises in Commercial Street in Pontypool as part of Operation CeCe, during which significant quantities of illicit tobacco, cigarettes and illegal vapes were found hidden in a concealed storage area behind an unused fridge unit.
Further illegal products were later recovered from a vehicle linked to the business.
Tahsin Mokhtar, from Cardiff, was sentenced to a total of 28 months imprisonment for carrying on a fraudulent business contrary to the Fraud Act 2006, offences under the Trade Marks Act 1994 and for breaching a closure order issued under the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014.
Arish Mohammedi, from Cardiff, was sentenced to 30 months imprisonment for carrying on a fraudulent business.
A forfeiture and destruction order for the illegal products was also made.
Daniel Morelli, joint assistant director public protection and environment, said: “This prosecution demonstrates our commitment to taking robust action against those who break the law and seek to profit from unlawful trading practices.
“Illegal tobacco and vapes have been found to contain a range of substances, which can be harmful to health. The stern penalties imposed demonstrate that the Courts take these offences seriously.”

items.body:
In a UK supermarket first, Morrisons is making Christmas shopping even easier by launching new in-store technology that helps customers quickly find exactly what they’re looking for.
The new ‘shop to light’ feature uses blinking electronic shelf labels, installed by Vusion, to help shoppers locate products quickly and easily. To use the feature, customers simply need to open the Product Finder tool on the homepage of their More Card app, search for the product they need and select ‘flash price label’. The app will share the in-store location, ask the customer to confirm if they are in the right aisle, and then the corresponding digital shelf label will flash magenta, making it easier for the customer to spot the exact product they want.
Already a popular feature in the United States, the new technology is being rolled out exclusively to Morrisons stores as they are installed with digital shelf edge labels, currently over 270 of its supermarkets have them – just in time for the Christmas trolley dash.
Whether customers are picking up last-minute Christmas essentials or searching for a specific ingredient, the new tool takes the guesswork out of finding the right product, helping customers get everything they need for the festive season with less time spent browsing aisles.
The feature is ideal for navigating high-density product aisles like herbs, spices, or sauces, as well as locating popular seasonal items such as cranberry sauce.
Morrisons has partnered with Vusion to digitise pricing across its entire supermarket estate using electronic shelf labels to automate price updates and improve pricing accuracy.
Gordon Macpherson, group productivity director at Morrisons said: “We know that Christmas is one of the busiest times of the year for our customers, and we’re always looking for new ways to make their shopping experience as easy and convenient as possible. Our new ‘shop to light’ feature is a great example of how we’re using technology to make a real difference in-store, helping our customers find the products they need quickly, whether they’re shopping for their Christmas dinner or just popping in to pick up a few last-minute essentials.”
Roy Horgan, UK & Ireland CEO at Vusion, said: “Technology has a huge role to play in making the shopping journey simpler, faster and more enjoyable for customers. ‘Shop to light’ is a great example of how we can help customers find what they need while making stores more seamless. Morrisons has been a fantastic partner in embracing innovation, and we are incredibly proud to be working together to help shape the future of retail.”
The Product Finder function is now available directly on the More Card app homepage, making it easier than ever for customers to access useful shopping tools in the app.

items.body:
SRT Group, parent company of leading last-mile delivery platform Stuart, today announces its acquisition by ambitious UK technology firm Quiver.
Founded in Paris in 2015, Stuart has grown rapidly, particularly in on-demand food, grocery and retail delivery across the UK, France and Poland.
The brainchild of two UK tech entrepreneurs, Quiver has garnered a reputation as a profitable, high margin business model, providing a best-in-class technology platform to high-street retailers.
Together, the two companies’ combined expertise will deliver greater value to enterprise and retail, grocery and food delivery clients across Europe and support market-leading innovation in last-mile delivery.
The deal involved Quiver acquiring SRT Group from Munich-based private equity holding company Mutares. Following a successful three-year partnership under Mutares’ stewardship, Stuart streamlined its operations and built a strong foundation for its next phase of growth. The company is now well positioned to scale and is on track to achieve independent profitability by early 2027.
The deal includes significant new investment in Stuart’s operations and technology to support the expansion of its instant and scheduled offering with the launch of new brands, and to improve the experience for clients and courier partners.
Quiver’s model provides retailers with a holistic delivery service that offers them the convenience of delivering to consumers directly from stores, or via Quiver’s urban fulfillment centres. With its expertise built by focusing on major cities, the deal now means Quiver can lean into Stuart’s geographical reach in the UK, France and other European markets such as Poland. In return, the Quiver platform’s ability to provide couriers with highly productive and efficient, batched routes/sequences will give both companies the clear edge on competitors.
Stuart and Quiver will remain independent brands in the medium term, collaborating on tech, ops, and commercial strategies to deliver better value to retail, grocery and food delivery clients and expand into high-end retail.
“The European delivery landscape is gaining a formidable new alliance. We’re thrilled to start this new chapter working with the Quiver team,” said Cornelia Raportaru, CEO of Stuart. “Stuart is in a stronger position than ever. This fresh energy, direction and technical capability proven with retail partners will enable us to deliver even more innovation and better service, shaping the future of last-mile logistics across any type of business.”
“We’ve spent the last four years building a technology platform for retail; making ship-from-store, returns and exchanges really work for brands and their customers. Bringing Stuart into the business gives us scale, talent and a new roster of clients that helps us take the service to new sectors and new markets,” said Matthew Barrie, co-founder of Quiver. “With its geographical reach and heritage in the grocery, food and quick service restaurant sectors, Stuart is the perfect fit.”

items.title: Poundland secures more time to avert collapse
items.summary: Poundland has secured extra time to avert collapse after the directors of the struggling retailer managed to hold off its creditors by another 10 days. The high street chain’s management has filed a second notice to appoint administrators, which it is hoped will give its owners Gordon Brothers more time to find a buyer for [...]
items.body:
Poundland secures more time to avert collapse
Poundland has secured extra time to avert collapse after the directors of the struggling retailer managed to hold off its creditors by another 10 days.
The high street chain’s management has filed a second notice to appoint administrators, which it is hoped will give its owners Gordon Brothers more time to find a buyer for its 600 stores and 12,000 staff.
This comes after Gordon Brothers was slammed by MPs for “jeopardising thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets” during a two-hour grilling in Parliament on Wednesday.
A spokesperson for Poundland’s board said: “Over the past two weeks, Poundland has been operating under the statutory protection of a Notice of Intention (NOI) to appoint Administrators.
“Amid an ongoing sale process, and with funding agreed to enable the business to continue trading during this period, the Board of Poundland has today resolved to make an application for a second NOI with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people.”
The discount retailer said its stores will remain open during the 10-day moratorium on its creditors, as it thanked its colleagues, suppliers and customers “for their incredible and continued support”.
Talks continue for rescue buyer
Poundland’s founder, Steve Smith, had been warning in recent days that the retailer would not be able to continue trading as he accused Gordon Brothers of withholding the company’s access to the funds needed to pay its suppliers.
Gordon Brothers agreed to release £10m to Poundland as the first in a series of payments earlier this week, and its Europe chief, Mark Newton-Jones told MPs on Wednesday that the firm had in no way restricted the retailer’s access to funds.
But following the hearing the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne, said there were “concerning signs [Poundland had] been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run up to Christmas”.
Sources close to the hearing said that Newton-Jones appeared “exasperated at the media coverage” of the sale process and “tried to paint Gordon Brothers as the saviour of the situation”.
Another questioned whether Gordon Brothers is committed to finding a buyer who will keep the company intact, telling City AM it was “abundantly clear” the retailer’s owner gordon “will make vastly more money if it is broken up”.
The retailers’ future now hangs in the balance as talks continue with three bidders, NCP-owner Martin Property Group, little-known investor Xyra Group and Irish investment firm Innovest Holdings, it is understood.
Retailers including Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland, The Range and Poundstretcher are waiting in the wings to snap up Poundland’s stores and stock if it falls into administration.
A collapse of Poundland would be the most significant to hit the retail sector in years and would strike a blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive the high street.
“The truth is that too many high streets have been left to hollow out, leaving town centres a shell of what they once were,” Burnham said in September. “That must change.”
A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “We support the Board’s decision to extend the legal moratorium over the company by a further ten working days. This brings additional stability amid an ongoing sale process in the backdrop of increasing cost pressures and a difficult inflationary economic environment.
“With this decision, we are today able to confirm to Poundland employees that funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.”

Costa Coffee has agreed a decade-long extension of its partnership with leading retailer NEXT, securing the future of a relationship that has grown from a single concession location in 2011 to more than 140 stores nationwide today.
The new agreement, which extends the partnership until January 2036, builds on more than 15 years of successful collaboration and reflects the strength of customer demand, continued investment across the estate and a shared commitment to continued growth.
Today, Costa Coffee operates more than 140 stores within NEXT locations across the UK, with the partnership continuing to expand through new openings, and ongoing investment.
During 2026, Costa Coffee opened seven new stores within NEXT locations, including a 3,000 sq ft store at NEXT’s flagship destination in Bluewater. The store is Costa Coffee’s largest within the NEXT estate and one of the first to feature the brand’s latest store design, highlighting both businesses continued focus on meeting evolving consumer needs.
Costa Coffee has also refreshed 26 existing stores across the NEXT estate this year, further enhancing the customer experience and supporting the long-term success of the partnership.
Since first partnering in 2011, Costa Coffee and NEXT have steadily expanded their footprint together. The new agreement provides a strong foundation to continue building on that success over the next decade.
Tom Falk, head of property at Costa Coffee said: “NEXT has been a valued partner for many years and we’re delighted to extend our relationship through to 2036. This milestone reflects the strength of our partnership and creates an exciting platform for future growth.
“Together, we’ve grown from a single location to a network of more than 140 stores, adapting to changing consumer needs and investing in great coffee experiences along the way. The success of landmark locations such as Bluewater demonstrates what can be achieved when two customer-focused brands work together with a shared ambition. This agreement gives us a fantastic opportunity to build on that momentum in the years ahead.”

Marks & Spencer and Global Fashion Group today announce a new partnership to expand the reach of M&S Fashion across Asia Pacific, making it easier for more customers to shop M&S through leading local platforms and an improved, regionally fulfilled shopping experience.
M&S has launched on ZALORA in Southeast Asia, offering customers a curated selection of the best of M&S Fashion across womenswear, menswear, kidswear and lingerie. In early 2027, M&S will launch on THE ICONIC in Australia and New Zealand. GFG will also fulfil M&S.com orders for customers in Australia, with the potential to scale this service to other markets.
Through GFG’s multi-channel fulfilment network, M&S inventory will be held in a single stock pool in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, with orders fulfilled within the region rather than shipped from the UK. This will provide a more seamless customer experience across THE ICONIC, ZALORA and M&S.com in Australia, with faster delivery and returns, while improving the availability of M&S product.
The partnership is another step forward in M&S’s international strategy to build a more sustainable, profitable global business through strong strategic partnerships and simple, scalable operating models. Combining GFG’s established platforms, regional infrastructure and marketing capabilities with the strength of the M&S brand and product offer will enable M&S to reach more customers and create a platform for future growth across Asia Pacific.
Mark Lemming, managing director of International at M&S, said: “Our ambition is to leverage M&S as a trusted global brand, driving growth through capital light, scalable partnerships. Online growth is a key part of how we reach more customers around the world and this partnership with GFG gives customers across Asia Pacific more ways to shop the best of M&S, while improving the experience through faster, regionally fulfilled delivery.”
Christoph Barchewitz, CEO of GFG, said: “This important partnership shows the opportunities available when a global brand leverages infrastructure purposefully built for this region. M&S customers across Asia Pacific will now get faster delivery, easier returns and broader access without M&S needing to manage a local fulfilment centre and carrier network. That removes the biggest barriers to entering and expanding in the region, and we see significant scope to extend it further.”

New IGD research commissioned by Instacart, drawing on 5,000 shoppers, 40 accompanied shopping trips and retailer […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
For grocery retailers, keeping pace with retail technology means understanding which investments will actually deliver the greatest value for their shoppers. Shoppers surveyed say they favor grocery retailers that help them save time, save money and stay in control. New IGD research commissioned by Instacart, drawing on 5,000 shoppers, 40 accompanied shopping trips and retailer interviews across the UK, France, Germany, Spain and Italy, shows where to start.
According to the research, European grocery shoppers surveyed aren’t asking for more technology – they’re asking for less effort. The opportunity for retailers is not simply to add more technology to the journey, but instead, use it to remove the friction shoppers experience across planning, finding, choosing and paying. Read on for some of the key insights, or download the full report.
Make shopping easier, not simply smarter
Across the five countries surveyed, shoppers’ priorities are broadly consistent. Those surveyed rate the basics that make their grocery shop easier as the most important, including: freshness and getting the right products, finding the best value, locating products easily, controlling total spend, confidence in stock and access to relevant offers. More novelty capabilities like discovering new products and meal inspiration fall lower in the ranks.
For the shoppers in this research, friction rarely sits in one isolated moment. It accumulates across planning, finding, choosing, comparing and paying. An unavailable product, a confusing offer or an unexpected intervention at checkout may each be manageable on its own; together, they can turn a routine shop into a frustrating experience. Checkout is the most cited in-store pain point. Online, where consumers can compare retailers and switch more easily, repeated challenges and annoyances may lead them to order less often or move their grocery spend elsewhere.
Personalise to save shoppers money, without taking control away
The shoppers surveyed are not rejecting personalisation or AI. They are defining the terms on which it works best: when technology saves money, saves time, remembers something useful or helps them compare credible options. Saving money is consistently the strongest use case for technology.
That shows up clearly in what online shoppers surveyed want from an AI grocery assistant on a retailer’s website or app. Around three in five say the most appealing features are those that help them stay within budget (58.7%), see relevant offers (58.2%), find cheaper alternatives (57.4%) and compare products more easily (57.0%). Reminders for forgotten essentials and substitution recommendations are a useful second layer, appealing to just over half of shoppers.
However, they still want the final say. Around four in five say they want to stay in charge of what they buy even when technology helps. As an example, automatically pre-filling a basket is the weakest proposition in every market (39.3%). As one French consumer put it: “I want AI to help me, but not do it for me.” Among those surveyed, current AI use is still limited and varies by age, so retailers need to demonstrate a clear, practical benefit first.
One set of needs, five market opportunities
Shoppers surveyed in all five countries prioritise the same basics, but start from different places. The same feature can solve a different problem, depending on the mission and market.
- UK: 28% of UK shoppers surveyed say they regularly shop both in-store and online, the highest omnichannel behavior of the five countries. The opportunity is connecting planning, shopping and payment.
- France: French online shoppers surveyed are split almost evenly between delivery and click and collect. They also state a preference for light-touch help: “Not crossing that thin line between helping and telling you what to do.”
- Germany: more than 80% of German shoppers surveyed say they shop mainly in-store, and time saving, organised routes and technical reliability come first.
- Spain: Spanish shoppers surveyed show high interest in new tools, but 62% worry personalised recommendations are designed to make them spend more. Technology should clearly help shoppers save money and stay in control.
- Italy: more than 80% of Italian shoppers surveyed say they shop mainly in-store, and 65% say they’re open to technology when it solves a clear shopping problem. They were also more likely than shoppers in other countries to say they’d change where they shop after a poor experience.
Fix, connect, innovate
The research points to a clear sequence for retailers: fix and connect, then innovate. Fix the basics that break trust first, especially availability, substitutions, fresh quality, search, promotions and checkout reliability. Advanced features will only create value if these basics work. Then connect information across channels, so lists, preferences, offers and purchase history move with the customer. Only then introduce new technology where the benefit is clear and the operation is ready.
As one Chief Technology Officer in Spain put it: “Use technology to solve the problems that you already know the user has.”
Make it easier, and the rest follows
Grocery shoppers will value retailers that help them save time, save money and stay in control. The research suggests that the winners will not be the retailers with the most technology, but rather those that deploy it most effectively to simplify the customer journey, strengthen trust at every touchpoint and deliver a more connected, consistent and personalised experience. The research shows where to start: fix the basics, connect the journey, then innovate where the benefit is clear. Instacart Enterprise brings together ecommerce, in-store technology and AI to help grocers do exactly that.
