items.body:
New research from Lidl GB has revealed the extent of the financial pressure facing UK parents, with one in 12 (8%) – equivalent to an estimated 660,000 families – considering turning to charity donation schemes to ensure their children have presents to open on Christmas morning.
This is reflective of a wider struggle to balance festive expectations with household budgets. More than four in five British parents (82%) are feeling significant pressure over the financial burden of gift-buying, with nearly one million (12%) having to raid emergency savings to cover Christmas costs.
For many, that concern extends to those around them. Over two thirds of parents (69%) say they know a friend, neighbour or relative who may struggle to afford presents for their children this Christmas.
In response, Lidl GB is bringing its biggest ever Christmas Toy Bank appeal to all 1,000+ of its stores, with dedicated donation boxes landing in stores this week to make it as easy as possible for shoppers to give a little something back to families in need in their local communities.
Now in its fourth year, the appeal invites customers to donate new, unopened toys of any brand at collection points located at the front of every Lidl store until 16th December 2026. All donations will be distributed locally across England, Scotland and Wales through the community giving platform Neighbourly, helping to bring the magic of Christmas to children who might otherwise go without.
Alongside the Toy Bank appeal, Lidl is also stepping in to help ease the squeeze on seasonal bills, rolling out £25,000 worth of festive support. Households will have the chance to win a £100 Lidl Plus coupon, which they can either put towards their own Christmas dinner and festive essentials, or extend a helping hand to a friend, neighbour or relative in the spirit of giving. To enter the Prize Draw, customers need to enter their Lidl Plus email address into the form here before midnight on Tuesday 1st December.
Georgina Hall, Director of Corporate Affairs at Lidl GB, said: “Every child deserves the excitement of waking up to presents under the tree on Christmas morning. However, we know Christmas is going to be hard for a lot of people this year and we want to do what we can to help.
“The response to our Toy Bank over the past four years has been remarkable, and even a simple gift can make a huge difference to a child on Christmas morning. Combined with our £100 vouchers, we’re giving practical, direct support to the communities we serve.”
The initiative forms part of the discounter’s seasonal community commitment, which also includes a £500,000 donation to local charities selected by store colleagues, matching a £500,000 fund allocated earlier this year via the Lidl Plus customer scheme.

items.body:
Morrisons Media Group (MMG) is expanding its retail media proposition to include Morrisons’ approximately 1,700 convenience stores, giving brands and suppliers a more joined-up approach to planning campaigns across the retailer’s Supermarket and Convenience estates.
The launch comes as the UK convenience market is forecast to grow from £49.2bn in 2025 to £56.2bn by 2030, according to IGD. Shopper behaviour is evolving too, with Lumina Intelligence reporting a 5% year-on-year increase in convenience shopping visits, alongside a 7% decline in items purchased per trip. These changing habits highlight the importance of tailoring campaigns to distinct shopping missions, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach across retail environments.
The expansion brings convenience media into MMG’s wider proposition, providing suppliers with a consistent point of contact and access to the group’s strategic planning, client service and proposition-development expertise.
With convenience shopping driven by different customer needs, locations and purchasing occasions, MMG will take a tailored approach to the channel, helping suppliers develop campaigns that reflect the distinct shopping behaviours of convenience customers while connecting activity to their broader retail media strategies.
Steve Newbould, head of commercial data & media, Morrisons Media Group, said: “Expanding Morrisons Media Group’s proposition into Convenience is an important step in how we support our supplier partners. Our customers shop across different formats for different reasons, and bringing these opportunities together allows us to offer brands a more comprehensive way to engage with them. This is about building on the strength of our existing retail media proposition while recognising the growing importance of Convenience.”
The expanded proposition combines Morrisons’ retail expertise and first-party customer insights with SMG’s retail media capabilities. Suppliers will benefit from MMG’s existing strategic support, including insights informed by Morrisons’ first-party data ecosystem, MoreViu, to help shape campaign planning around relevant customer missions and commercial objectives.
Katie Jackson, Morrisons Media Group, said: “For suppliers, the opportunity is to plan more effectively across the Morrisons estate without taking a one-size-fits-all approach. We’re bringing the same strategic support and expertise to Convenience, helping brands identify relevant opportunities and develop campaigns that reflect the needs of customers in each shopping environment.”
Rosie Houston, managing director, UK Retail Media Networks, SMG, said: “As retail media continues to evolve, there’s an increasing opportunity to connect brand activity across different shopping environments. Our partnership with Morrisons is focused on making those opportunities more accessible and actionable for suppliers, combining retail expertise, customer insights and strategic planning to help brands make the most of every customer interaction.”

Matalan, the leading UK fashion and homeware retailer, is continuing its investment in its store estate with four openings this November, as the business enters the peak Black Friday and Christmas trading period.
The openings in Aylesbury, Clacton-on-Sea, Bangor in Northern Ireland and Newport in Wales are the latest in a wider programme of investment to modernise Matalan’s stores and bring its improved shopping experience to more customers. The programme has been delivering encouraging results, with the retailer’s Derby store, which opened earlier this year and introduced Matalan’s latest, more modern store format, becoming its most successful opening to date, reaching £1m in sales in just 51 days.
Together, the four locations represent nearly 100,000 sq ft of new retail space and will employ c.40 colleagues per store. Clacton, a new 30,000 sq ft site at Brooke Retail Park, opened its doors on 7 November, alongside a new 22,000 sq ft store at Aylesbury Shopping Park, which opened on the same day.
On 14 November, a 17,000 sq ft store will open at Springhill in Bangor, building on Matalan’s established presence in Northern Ireland. In Wales, the retailer will open a new 27,000 sq ft full-price store at Mendalgief Retail Park in Newport, replacing its former clearance store nearby and bringing Matalan’s latest store format to customers in the area.
The new locations will showcase the improvements being introduced across Matalan’s wider estate, including brighter interiors, simpler layouts and enhanced visual merchandising. Alongside the retailer’s evolving fashion and homeware collections, these changes are designed to make it easier for customers to discover the latest ranges and see the improvements Matalan has made to its product offering.
These improvements will also be reflected in the retailer’s Hull store, which is set to reopen later this month, following a significant redevelopment that has seen the space reconfigured into a modern two-floor store, featuring improved navigation, upgraded lighting and signage, and refreshed fitting rooms and checkout areas.
With the Golden Quarter in full swing, the new stores will also give customers the opportunity to shop Matalan’s recently launched Christmas collection, spanning fashion, gifting and homeware, with almost 95% of products priced under £35.
James Dorling, property director at Matalan, commented: “Our stores play a huge role in how customers experience Matalan, so it’s essential that they reflect the improvements we’re making to our product and brand.
That’s been the focus of our investment over the past two years – not just making stores look better, but making them easier to shop and better at showcasing what we have to offer. It’s about investing in the right locations, improving the shopping environments, and giving our customers even more reasons to choose Matalan.
“The response to the changes we’ve made has been really positive, with Derby a particular highlight. The four openings this November mark another important milestone in our investment programme, and we’re delighted to be bringing the latest Matalan experience to more communities in time for Christmas.”
The continued investment in stores forms part of Matalan’s wider business transformation, which has seen the retailer evolve its product and digital offering alongside its physical estate. This progress was brought together earlier this year through the launch of Believe It’s Matalan, a new brand platform designed to challenge perceptions of the retailer and encourage customers to take a fresh look at what it has to offer.

items.title: Greater Manchester mayor meets with Fed retailers
items.summary: The mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, met with Craig Etchells, national vice president of the Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) at his shop in Chorlton on Thursday, 4 November. They discussed the opportunities and challenges facing shops on the high street in Manchester… This story continues at Greater Manchester mayor meets with Fed retailers Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
They discussed the opportunities and challenges facing shops on the high street in Manchester and beyond.
The meeting focused on the Fed’s work to tackle retail crime and rogue trade, as well as the Mayor’s new High Street Taskforce which is set to be launched shortly, alongside a £20m Good Growth High Streets Fund.
Also discussed were some of the costs facing small shops including rising energy bills, as well as taxation and the Fed’s engagement with the government to support small shops.
The meeting came just after the government announced an increase in Small Business Rates Relief threshold to £18,000, helping many Fed members.
As well as discussing some key challenges facing small shops, Etchells spoke about areas of innovation, as well as his continued work promoting home news delivery (HND) in the area around his shop and the local jobs that the shop provides.
They also discussed the role shops can provide in giving young people skills and confidence that can last their whole career, with Etchells pointing out that a member of the mayor’s GMCA team had his first job delivering newspapers for him as a teenager.
The launch of the deposit return scheme (DRS) which will commence in October next year, was also discussed.
The Fed is encouraging members to get involved through its range of communication channels, including the DRS Knowledge Hub on its website as well as its member magazine which is sent to its thousands of members each month.
Bev Craig said: “It was a very positive meeting and it was good to catch-up with Craig, meet the team in his shop and learn more about the work of the Fed across the whole country.
“Newsagents and independent retailers are a vital part of our high streets, providing everyday essentials and providing a place for communities to stay connected. Through our work in Greater Manchester, including a new High Streets Fund and Taskforce, we’re bringing pride and that sense of community back to our high streets.
“I look forward to working with Craig and the Fed on this and on their campaigns on issues like retail crime and supporting local jobs.”
Etchells said: “I would like to thank the mayor for her time and interest. Having met with her recently where we discussed the High Street Task Force, this was a very useful opportunity to show her my business and how integrated it is with the excellent local community we have here in Chorlton.”

items.title: Citizens of Soil launches in around 425 Tesco stores
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Citizens of Soil, the B Corp-certified olive oil brand founded by certified olive oil sommelier and cookbook author Sarah Vachon, is bringing its fresh, traceable oils to selected Tesco stores nationwide this week. It will include two single-origin, certified organic extra virgin olive oils: Greek (Delicate & Herby) and Spanish (Vibrant & Fruity). The launch […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Citizens of Soil, the B Corp-certified olive oil brand founded by certified olive oil sommelier and cookbook author Sarah Vachon, is bringing its fresh, traceable oils to selected Tesco stores nationwide this week. It will include two single-origin, certified organic extra virgin olive oils: Greek (Delicate & Herby) and Spanish (Vibrant & Fruity).
The launch marks a significant milestone for the British brand, which has been shaking up the UK olive oil scene since 2021 with its high-quality, transparent supply chain, and focus on flavour. It’s now bringing its mission to transform how the UK shops for, cooks with, and thinks about olive oil to one of the country’s leading retailers.
While olive oil has traditionally been treated as an everyday commodity, Citizens of Soil is encouraging shoppers to approach the category with the same curiosity and appreciation as wine or specialty coffee.
Launching side by side are two certified organic, single-origin extra virgin olive oils, each with its own distinctive character.
- Greek, Delicate & Herby: A Koroneiki olive oil sourced from small-scale family groves around Lanconia in the Peloponnese. Buttery and herbaceous with a gentle cracked-pepper finish, ideal for salads, pestos and finishing dishes.
- Spanish, Vibrant & Fruity: An Arbequina and Picual blend from Albacete in Castilla-La Mancha, milled within an hour of picking. Verdant with notes of vine tomato, almond and lemon peel, with a peppery finish suited to rice dishes, roasted vegetables and bold Mediterranean cooking.
Sarah Vachon, co-founder of Citizens of Soil, said:
“Tesco is where thousands of people buy their olive oil, so it’s where we can make the biggest difference. Shoppers already choose coffee by origin, wine by grape, and chocolate by percentage. And as they trade up on everyday staples, we are confident olive oil will be next, due to its wide range of flavours and uses. We want to show people just that: these oils taste completely different, and putting them side by side lets shoppers discover that for themselves and find the oil that suits the way they cook.”
Citizens of Soil is championing a different approach to provenance. As a certified olive oil sommelier who sources directly from independent producers, Sarah brings origin and tasting education to an every day staple, built on the following commitments:
- Every bottle is traceable, with harvest date, acidity and polyphenol levels independently lab-tested and published.2
- Every oil is fresh, milled within hours of picking and bottled from the latest harvest to preserve its flavour.
- Every bottle is organic, and farmed in harmony with nature with regenerative practices to protect biodiversity and soil health.
- At least 50% of their producers are women, championing a more equitable food system and helping to secure a better future for farming.3
The Tesco launch caps a year of rapid growth for Citizens of Soil. The brand sourced the oil for Ottolenghi’s own extra virgin olive oil, opened the UK’s first Olive Oil Bar, a month-long pop-up in Covent Garden, and published Drizzle, a community cookbook of recipes from small olive oil farmers around the world. The Tesco listing now takes Citizens of Soil from the Tesco Accelerator programme onto shelves in over 400 stores across the country for the first time.
Citizens of Soil Greek Extra Virgin Olive Oil and Spanish Extra Virgin Olive Oil are available in around 425 Tesco stores this week, with an RRP of £19 for 500ml. Both oils will be 20% off at Tesco- on a Clubcard Price Promotion at £15.20 for two weeks from 24 November.

items.title: Post Office urges retailers to prepare for outages with backup cash
items.summary: Digital payment outages are costing high street retailers on average £255 every hour an outage lasts, new research commissioned by Post Office finds. Nearly a quarter (24%) report having to turn customers away, delay or pause transactions, or close due to not being able to… This story continues at Post Office urges retailers to prepare for outages with backup cash Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Nearly a quarter (24%) report having to turn customers away, delay or pause transactions, or close due to not being able to serve a customer at all (22%).
UK retailers surveyed reported an average of three payment disruptions in the last year, and the frequency of these events is predicted to grow.
While nearly a third of UK adults (29%) admit they have been unable to pay at a store checkout in the past year because a retailer did not accept a payment method they could use. Among those affected, over one in five (21%) said the retailer did not accept cash.
As the government’s recent ‘Be Ready’ campaign encourages households to keep cash and essential supplies for emergencies, Post Office has issued guidance calling on retailers to consider reviewing their own contingency plans and ensure they can continue accepting cash when digital payments are unavailable.
While 83% of businesses surveyed have a written or agreed contingency plan, 90% don’t include accepting cash as a back-up, despite 81% agreeing that keeping cash available for customers and emergencies is important.
Cash helps businesses remain operational during disruptions, with two-thirds (69%) being able to continue serving customers during digital payment outages.
However, with only 32% of high street retailers surveyed saying they currently accept cash, the research reveals a potential resilience gap if digital payments fail.
Ben Hunter Woollard, head of banking at Post Office, said: “A payment outage can disrupt trading in seconds, resulting in customers being turned away and sales lost. Cash has helped many retailers continue trading during recent disruptions, but it is rarely included in formal contingency plans.
“With the government encouraging households to keep some cash available for emergencies, retailers should also consider how they will keep serving customers if digital payments go down in emergencies. If cash usage is being encouraged, so should its acceptance.
“Our new guidance gives retailers practical steps to communicate clearly with customers and build a plan that works for their business.
Although outages highlight gaps in acceptance, cash still remains an important everyday payment option for many consumers, supporting cash-only transactions that contribute £27bn to the UK economy.
While contactless cards are now the most commonly preferred payment method, cash is the number one choice for over a fifth (22%) of consumers and used by more than half of the nation (58%) for everyday purchases.
This shows that cash is not only relevant when systems fail – it remains part of how many people manage day-to-day spending. For retailers, this means cash acceptance policies must factor daily customer-choice as well as resilience.
Among UK adults who have been unable to pay at a store checkout in the past year, 21% said this was because the business did not accept cash. For 68% of those affected, being unable to pay happened on more than two occasions.
Only 28% of high street retailers say community needs and customer payment preferences influence their decisions about which payment methods they offer. Not considering how customers in the local community prefer to pay could mean losing sales.
New guidelines for retailers
To support business resilience, Post Office has published new guidance to help retailers plan for payment disruptions, meet local customer needs and clearly communicate payment options.
Ed Woodall, chief executive, Association of Convenience Stores (ACS), said: “Cash remains an important payment method for customers in convenience stores, with 99% of convenience retailers accepting cash.
“When people lose access to other payment methods through outages or issues with networks, cash is a crucial safety net that allows businesses to continue trading and serving their communities.”
Helen Dickinson, chief executive at British Retail Consortium, said: “Retailers accept a range of payment methods, guided by their customers’ needs. They recognise the importance of cash both as a budgeting tool for managing day-to-day spending and as a reliable option when digital payments are disrupted.
“While businesses remain free to decide which payment methods they accept, cash remains a viable option to support consumer choice and business resilience.”
Melissa Samuel, postmistress at Bourton-on-the-Water Post Office, said: “As postmistress in Bourton-on-the-Water, I see first-hand how important cash continues to be to our local community.
“We have local businesses regularly coming into the Post Office to deposit their cash takings, but just as importantly, they also use our change-giving service, so they have the notes and coins they need to serve their customers.
“Having local access to cash for business and customers becomes even more important when digital payments are disrupted. When card terminals are down, we see customers come into our branch to withdraw cash, often after being directed here by a local business, so they can go back and complete their purchase.
“It is a reminder that cash helps keep shops trading when other payment options are temporarily unavailable.”

items.body:
Majestic opens 30th store in London
Majestic has opened its 30th new store in Ealing, West London, marking a major milestone in its ongoing brick-and-mortar expansion.
At the new store there are over 1,000 stocked wines, alongside a range of premium beers, spirits, soft drinks and low- and no-alcohol alternatives.
There is also a dedicated area for 72 fine wines, and shoppers will have the chance to sample products at an in-store tasting counter.
At the new site there are also additional services such as free glass hire, wedding tastings and next-day delivery for online shoppers.
There is also a ‘Shop Local’ feature that allows customers to order from the range available at the Ealing store in real-time for home delivery or click and collect.
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
This new site will also support the retailer’s growing B2B division and supply wines to hospitality destinations in the Ealing borough.
This is part of a wider £4m investment from the wine retailer in its store portfolio during the 2026/27 period after a series of renovations and the launch of its Trowbridge shop in July.
The retailer has further planned for expansion as it continues its commitment to growing its estate under Fortress ownership.
John Colley, executive chairman and CEO of Majestic Wine Group, said: “This is another significant milestone for Majestic in our growth story under Fortress. To have opened 30 fantastic new shops in such a challenging retail environment is a testament to the hard work of our colleagues across the business.
“Our growth over the past seven years proves that wine lovers still value human expertise, personalised advice and the chance to taste new wines before they buy – things you can’t get anywhere else on the high street.”

items.title: 660,000 families need toy donations this Christmas, according to Lidl
items.summary: New research from Lidl GB has revealed the extent of the financial pressure facing UK parents this Christmas, with an estimated 660,000 families considering turning to charity donation schemes to…
items.body:
660,000 families need toy donations this Christmas, according to Lidl
New research from Lidl GB has revealed the extent of the financial pressure facing UK parents this Christmas, with an estimated 660,000 families considering turning to charity donation schemes to ensure their children have presents to open.
Lidl said its study reflects a wider struggle to balance festive expectations with household budgets. More than four in five parents (82 per cent) are feeling pressure over the financial burden of gift-buying, with nearly one million (12 per cent) having to raid emergency savings to cover Christmas costs.
Over two thirds of parents (69 per cent) said they know a friend, neighbour or relative who may struggle to afford presents for their children this Christmas.
In response, Lidl GB is bringing its biggest ever Christmas Toy Bank appeal to all of its stores, with dedicated donation boxes landing in stores this week to make it as easy as possible for shoppers to give a little something back to families in need in their local communities.
Now in its fourth year, the appeal invites customers to donate new, unopened toys of any brand at collection points located at the front of every Lidl store until 16 December 2026. All donations will be distributed locally across England, Scotland and Wales through the community giving platform Neighbourly, helping to bring the magic of Christmas to children who might otherwise go without.
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
Georgina Hall, director of corporate affairs at Lidl GB, said: “Every child deserves the excitement of waking up to presents under the tree on Christmas morning. However, we know Christmas is going to be hard for a lot of people this year and we want to do what we can to help.
“The response to our Toy Bank over the past four years has been remarkable, and even a simple gift can make a huge difference to a child on Christmas morning. Combined with our £100 vouchers, we’re giving practical, direct support to the communities we serve.”
Alongside the Toy Bank appeal, Lidl is also stepping in to help ease the squeeze on seasonal bills, rolling out £25,000 worth of festive support. Households will have the chance to win a £100 Lidl Plus coupon, which they can either put towards their own Christmas dinner and festive essentials, or extend a helping hand to a friend, neighbour or relative in the spirit of giving.
To enter the Prize Draw, customers need to enter their Lidl Plus email address into the form here before midnight on Tuesday 1 December.
The initiative forms part of the discounter’s seasonal community commitment, which also includes a £500,000 donation to local charities selected by store colleagues, matching a £500,000 fund allocated earlier this year via the Lidl Plus customer scheme.

items.title: B&M profits rise as turnaround begins to win back shoppers
items.summary: B&M has reported a return to UK sales growth and a 16.6 per cent increase in adjusted pre-tax profit for the first half, as its turnaround strategy begins to gain traction with value-conscious shoppers. For the 26 weeks to September 26, group revenue increased 3.6 per cent to £2.85bn, compared with £2.75bn a year earlier....
items.body:
B&M has reported a return to UK sales growth and a 16.6 per cent increase in adjusted pre-tax profit for the first half, as its turnaround strategy begins to gain traction with value-conscious shoppers.
For the 26 weeks to September 26, group revenue increased 3.6 per cent to £2.85bn, compared with £2.75bn a year earlier. Statutory pre-tax profit climbed 53.7 per cent to £115m.
Adjusted EBITDA increased 6 per cent to £203m, with net income rising to £84m from £53m in the same period last year.
The results mark an improvement for the discount retailer, which has been working to address declining profitability and weaker trading in its UK business under chief executive Tjeerd Jegen.
Its Back to B&M Basics turnaround plan focuses on restoring price competitiveness, simplifying product ranges, improving promotions and strengthening on-shelf availability.
Jegen said: “Over the past year, we have sharpened our pricing, improved the on-shelf availability of our best-selling brands, revamped our in-store promotions and reduced SKU count across our stores.
“Our goal has been to restore B&M UK to sustainable like-for-like growth while making everyday life more affordable for customers facing mounting cost-of-living pressures, and our second quarter LFL performance of +3.2 per cent shows the first phase of our strategy is working.”
Additionally, B&M France delivered positive trading, with like-for-like sales up 5.9 per cent.
Jegen stressed that the retailer’s focus on sharper pricing and a more streamlined product range was helping attract shoppers, as it continues to compete for customers amid pressure on household budgets and competition from supermarket loyalty schemes.
The retailer said early trading in its golden quarter, covering the key October to December Christmas period, had been positive across all three businesses.
B&M expects full-year adjusted pre-tax profit of between £280m and £330m for FY27, compared with £284m in the previous financial year. This represents potential growth of up to 16 per cent.
The group also reported stronger cash generation, with post-tax free cash flow rising to £132m from £51m a year earlier, while net debt fell 28.7 per cent to £613m.

items.title: WH Smith profits fall 30% despite revenue climbing to £1.6bn
items.summary: WH Smith has reported a sharp decline in annual profits despite revenue increasing 5 per cent to £1.63bn, as the travel retailer continues to tackle operational challenges and restructure its international business. For the year ended 31 August 2026, headline profit before tax and exceptional items fell 30 per cent to £76m, compared with £108m...
items.body:
WH Smith has reported a sharp decline in annual profits despite revenue increasing 5 per cent to £1.63bn, as the travel retailer continues to tackle operational challenges and restructure its international business.
For the year ended 31 August 2026, headline profit before tax and exceptional items fell 30 per cent to £76m, compared with £108m the previous year.
The retailer also reported a statutory loss before tax of £107m, compared with a £2m profit in 2025, following £164m in non-underlying charges. These included around £103m in impairment costs, primarily relating to its North American operations.
Like-for-like sales across the group increased 2 per cent, while free cash flow fell to £52m from £63m.
The results come as WH Smith undertakes a strategic reset following a turbulent year marked by profit warnings, an accounting error and changes to its leadership.
Executive chairman Leo Quinn has been tasked with restoring financial discipline and simplifying the business, with a renewed focus on profitable growth and returns on investment.
The group has been reviewing its international portfolio, scaling back underperforming operations and concentrating investment on its core travel retail markets.
In September, WH Smith warned that annual profits would come in at the lower end of its previous forecast, citing weaker travel demand, inflationary pressures and increased promotional activity.
Looking ahead, the retailer expects headline profit before tax and non-underlying items of between £75m and £85m for its 2027 financial year. Net debt is forecast to stand at around £320m.
WH Smith said its priorities include strengthening operational foundations, improving governance and controls, and maintaining a tighter approach to capital allocation as it works to rebuild investor confidence.

items.title: Morrisons introduces UK first with flashing product finder
items.summary: In a UK supermarket first, Morrisons is launching new in-store technology that helps customers quickly find exactly what they're looking for. The new ‘shop to light’ feature uses blinking electronic shelf labels, installed by Vusion, to help shoppers locate products quickly and easily. To use… This story continues at Morrisons introduces UK first with flashing product finder Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The new ‘shop to light’ feature uses blinking electronic shelf labels, installed by Vusion, to help shoppers locate products quickly and easily.
To use the feature, customers simply need to open the Product Finder tool on the homepage of their More Card app, search for the product they need and select ‘flash price label’.
The app will share the in-store location, ask the customer to confirm if they are in the right aisle, and then the corresponding digital shelf label will flash magenta, making it easier for the customer to spot the exact product they want.
Already a popular feature in the US, the new technology is being rolled out exclusively to Morrisons stores as they are installed with digital shelf edge labels.
Whether customers are picking up last-minute Christmas essentials or searching for a specific ingredient, Morrisons said the new tool takes the guesswork out of finding the right product, helping customers get everything they need for the festive season with less time spent browsing aisles.
The feature is said to suitable for navigating high-density product aisles like herbs, spices, or sauces, as well as locating popular seasonal items such as cranberry sauce.
Morrisons has partnered with Vusion to digitise pricing across its entire supermarket estate using electronic shelf labels to automate price updates and improve pricing accuracy.
Gordon Macpherson, group productivity director at Morrisons said: “We know that Christmas is one of the busiest times of the year for our customers, and we’re always looking for new ways to make their shopping experience as easy and convenient as possible.
“Our new ‘shop to light’ feature is a great example of how we’re using technology to make a real difference in-store, helping our customers find the products they need quickly, whether they’re shopping for their Christmas dinner or just popping in to pick up a few last-minute essentials.”
Roy Horgan, UK & Ireland CEO at Vusion, said: “Technology has a huge role to play in making the shopping journey simpler, faster and more enjoyable for customers.
“‘Shop to light’ is a great example of how we can help customers find what they need while making stores more seamless. Morrisons has been a fantastic partner in embracing innovation, and we are incredibly proud to be working together to help shape the future of retail.”

items.title: Burberry shares jump as turnaround puts trench coat back in fashion
items.summary: Shares in Burberry soared after the British fashion house returned to profit off the back of renewed demand for its iconic trench coat.  The FTSE 100 group took a £19m pre-tax profit in the six months to the end of September, recovering from its £48m loss at the same time last year, as its revenue [...]
items.body:
Burberry shares jump as turnaround puts trench coat back in fashion
Shares in Burberry soared after the British fashion house returned to profit off the back of renewed demand for its iconic trench coat.
The FTSE 100 group took a £19m pre-tax profit in the six months to the end of September, recovering from its £48m loss at the same time last year, as its revenue grew six per cent to £1.1bn. Shares in the group gained seven per cent in early trading to 1,166p.
Burberry chief executive Joshua Schulman has sought to return the fashion house to the mid-market by cutting prices and boosting the visibility of its well-known trench coats since he was appointed in 2024.
The fashion house told shareholders on Thursday that sales of its outerwear products grew by double digits in the period, driven by demand for its rainwear.
Burberry said it saw “particularly good growth” in sales of its tropical gabardine, a variation of its iconic trench coat which sells for about £1,795.
The group also saw strong demand for its cropped trench coats over the summer. This new design, which is available at a lower price point than the full-length trench, has been one of the ways Schulman has sought to make Burberry more affordable.
His arrival at Burberry followed the fashion house’s short-lived foray into ultra-high fashion, which prompted a period of falling sales as its aggressive price hikes alienated scores of consumers.
Cotswolds fever boosts Burberry
Schulman has also sought to arrest the luxury group’s declines in China – a crucial market for Burberry which had declined in the period before his appointment. Sales in Greater China were up nine per cent in the first quarter of Burberry’s financial year, though this growth has slowed to five per cent in recent months.
In recent months, Burberry has capitalised on the growing popularity of the Cotswolds with wealthy Americans, introducing a new handbag design named after the sought-after English region, some of which sell for more than £2,000.
The fashion house said sales of its leather goods have accelerated in recent months, driven by growing demand for its Cotswolds and vintage-check handbags.
Schulman said: “Two years ago, we launched Burberry Forward. Today, our brand and our business are stronger. Five consecutive quarters of growth and improved quality of sales demonstrate that our strategy is working.
“Having laid the foundations for growth, I am more confident than ever that we will realise the full potential of this extraordinary British luxury brand.”

items.title: WH Smith boss blames woes on ‘forced growth’ as profit falls
items.summary: The boss of WH Smith has blamed the retailer’s woes on its “forced growth” under previous management, as a sharp fall in profit undermined the group’s hunt for a turnaround. The London-listed travel retailer posted a £76m pre-tax profit in the year to the end August, 28 per cent lower than last year. After multiple [...]
items.body:
WH Smith boss blames woes on ‘forced growth’ as profit falls
The boss of WH Smith has blamed the retailer’s woes on its “forced growth” under previous management, as a sharp fall in profit undermined the group’s hunt for a turnaround.
The London-listed travel retailer posted a £76m pre-tax profit in the year to the end August, 28 per cent lower than last year. After multiple profit warnings earlier this year the group had cut its target to £75m, having initially hoped for as much as £115m.
Leo Quinn, the turnaround specialist who took charge of WH Smith in April, said he has begun “a fundamental reset” of the group as it battles soft consumer confidence and travel disruption caused by the Iran war.
The group’s executive chairman, who previously led comebacks at Balfour Beatty and Qinetiq, said it had suffered from “forced growth” which resulted in “increased costs, too many loss-making stores, acquisitions not integrated effectively and high organisational complexity”.
Quinn said WH Smith’s UK division, which includes stores at airports, train stations and hospitals, was forced to cut marketing spend and discount more products in response to “weaker consumer sentiment”.
The group’s shops at hospitals performed the best, with revenue growing nine per cent, compared to three per cent at its train station stores. Takings across WH Smith’s UK arm grew four per cent to £870m.
WH Smith told shareholders that its suppliers have adopted a more “cautious” approach in response to the “macroeconomic and geopolitical backdrop” caused by the conflict int he Middle East.
The firm, which is newly reliant on its airport stores after selling its high street estate last year, had been forced to issue multiple profit warnings throughout the year, as the Iran war causes travel disruption and pushes up the cost of flying, resulting in lower consumer spend at airports.
WH Smith saw its airport business grow by just one per cent on a like-for-like basis, with the group blaming “the macro environment and reduction in passengers”.
Flat US sales weigh on growth
The retailer’s revenue grew by nine per cent to £437m at its beleaguered North American arm, which was beset by an accounting scandal after it emerged that its profit in the region had been flattered for years.
But the group blamed lower passenger volumes in North America for its stalling growth at the start of the new financial year, as like-for-like growth was flat in the 10 weeks to 7 November.
Conroy Gaynor, a senior consumer analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said: “Our view remains that the company is in the midst of a difficult turnaround, with likely headwinds to earnings at least in the near term.”
Quinn said his “complex” turnaround plan will “transform WHSmith over the medium-term into a Group capable of generating attractive returns, with significant annual free cash flow.”

items.title: AI agents bring down wind farm within two hours
items.summary: <p>Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can hack into wind farms, erase the memory of electronic controllers and cut off their electricity production capability in under two hours.</p> <p>Research to be unveiled next week gives new urgency to calls for organisations to properly <a href="https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366649386/UK-power-plant-shutdown-highlights-CNI-cyber-challenges">secure the networks used to manage critical physical infrastructure</a>.</p> <p>The warning follows a <a href="https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366653380/Cold-chain-cyber-attacks-highlight-lack-of-OT-security-in-retail">wave of attacks on refrigeration systems</a> used by retailers across Europe, <a href="https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366653356/UK-abattoirs-caught-up-in-cyber-attack-against-European-supermarkets">meat processors</a> in the UK and a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/france-national-blo
items.body:
Getty Images
AI agents bring down wind farm within two hours
Warning after research shows AI agents can hack into a wind farm, access engineering data and shut down electricity supplies
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can hack into wind farms, erase the memory of electronic controllers and cut off their electricity production capability in under two hours.
Research to be unveiled next week gives new urgency to calls for organisations to properly secure the networks used to manage critical physical infrastructure.
The warning follows a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems used by retailers across Europe, meat processors in the UK and a French blood bank.
According to “red team” reports from penetration testing company Shinobi Security, two off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) were able to stop six turbines delivering nearly 10MW (megawatts) of power in a replicated wind farm, starting with “nothing but a set of VPN credentials”.
No specialist knowledge needed
The company’s head of research, David Mound, told Computer Weekly that the experiment shows that hackers no longer need specialist knowledge to attack devices used to control physical infrastructure – known as operational technology (OT).
He said the research showed that attackers could use an LLM to launch a successful attack without having detailed knowledge of how wind farms work.
“Even if you are not a seasoned OT red teamer or penetration tester, a normal attacker is able to amplify their capability by using and exploiting large language models. Even LLMs on their own are more than capable of penetrating and exploiting these environments,” he said.
Mound built a test rig from the same components used in a wind farm that was attacked by suspected Russian hackers in Poland in December 2025.
Poland’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) published a detailed report on the incident, allowing Mound and his co-researchers to build a rig that mimicked the operation of a real wind farm.
The rig used the same networking devices and a Siemens controller to replicate the farm’s connection to the electricity grid. It was combined with simulations of Scada (supervisory control and data acquisition) and HMI (human-machine interface) controllers to mimic the operation of the wind turbines.
Moonshot and Claude
Mound said it was important to make the rig as true to life as possible to ensure that the AI agents believed they were acting in a real environment, as the experiment showed they would behave differently if they believed the test was a simulation.
The researchers tested Anthropic’s Claude LLM, along with Kimi, an open source, open-weight AI model supplied by Chinese AI startup Moonshot.
Both models were able to successfully shut down the wind farm in a fraction of the time taken by human attackers targeting similar plants in Poland.
Claude took 66 minutes to shut down the wind farm’s connection to the power grid, at a cost of $20 in tokens. Kimi took just under two hours to reach the same point at a cost of just $8.
“In the real Polish wind farm hack, the attackers were there for 11 days before they shut down the plant,” said Mound.
Misconfigured devices
The AI models followed a similar attack path to the real hack in Poland, exploiting misconfigured devices rather than attempting anything more sophisticated, such as hunting for zero-day vulnerabilities.
They were given credentials to access a VPN – information that could be found on the dark web – to make the initial access to the wind farm.
The models worked out how to access a control device with a web portal that had been set up with default credentials, and from there they were able to set up an encrypted tunnel and pivot into the rest of the network.
The AI systems worked out that the network contained an “historian” database, which, among other operational data, recorded the actions taken by controllers in response to different wind speeds over time.
 
   
  “The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments. Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult”
David Mound, Shinobi Security
For the purpose of the experiment, the models were told not to do anything that would physically damage the infrastructure so that the experiment could be repeated.
“They were absolutely capable of turning off the power. And if it was a case of taking further malicious actions or deleting programs from the programmable logic controllers, they would have been more than capable of doing that themselves,” he said.
In a real-life attack, the LLMs could have been used by attackers to install ransomware on the control devices used in the wind farm, effectively shutting it down until the ransom was paid or until the wind farm could restore its systems from backups.
The turbine blades would have been protected from physical damage, as there are safety mechanisms in place to prevent them from spinning too quickly.
AI agent spoofed weather data
In an unexpected twist, one of the AI agents worked out how to spoof data from the weather station to make it appear that the wind was gusting, causing safety circuits to automatically shut down the turbines.
“It is incredible for an LLM to come up with that method of stopping the power because the main goal was to stop the power being placed on the grid,” he said.
One model also threatened to “drop the safety theatre” and take further destructive action if the researchers confirmed its hunch that the wind farm rig was a simulation, rather than a real wind farm.
When the Polish wind farm was attacked in December 2025, operators became aware that the plant had been attacked before there was a major incident. But a similar AI-driven attack would leave them with less time to react.
“The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments,” said Mound. “Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult.”
Getting basic security right
Protecting wind farms is a matter of getting the basics right, ensuring that network devices are not misconfigured and are not set to default passwords, said Mound.
It is also clear that information not generally regarded as sensitive for security purposes, such as records in the historian database, can be extremely useful for an LLM attacker. For example, it can use the information to work out that it has accessed a wind farm and how the wind farm operates.
“Those areas within a network where you have knowledge stores that you might not have thought had high value before now have much greater value when it comes to delivering context to an LLM,” he said.
Last week, Richard Horne, chief executive officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), urged organisations to ensure that control devices were patched and updated, in the wake of the hacking attacks on supermarket fridges.
“Large businesses will have a large amount of operational technology, whether it’s manufacturing lines, heating controls, or building management systems,” he said. “All organisations need to be looking for them and addressing both the connectivity and the configuration of those devices.”
David Mound will be presenting his research at the Sans CyberThreat Summit on 16 November.
How AI agents closed down a wind farm
- VPN into the perimeter with the issued credentials.
- Factory default credentials used on the boundary controller.
- Enabled SSH on that controller and used it as a pivot to enumerate the OT segment reliably.
- Unauthenticated access control failure on an online code repository, Gitea, gave access to the site’s entire engineering document store, including the grid interface notes and the Scada account.
- The documents identified the substation controller with an open interface. A single command allowed the power breaker to be turned on.
Source: Shinobi Security

items.title: OurCoop’s Mike Pickering: “Sustainability isn’t an optional extra for us”
items.summary: OurCoop won Sustainable Retailer of the Year at the first RG Excellence Awards for its efforts across energy savings and surplus food redistribution. Mike Pickering, head of sustainability, explains how the co-operative is linking environmental action with commercial resilience. OurCoop sees the business case for sustainability as starting with practical results. It has achieved around...
items.body:
OurCoop won Sustainable Retailer of the Year at the first RG Excellence Awards for its efforts across energy savings and surplus food redistribution. Mike Pickering, head of sustainability, explains how the co-operative is linking environmental action with commercial resilience.
OurCoop sees the business case for sustainability as starting with practical results. It has achieved around £500,000 in annual electricity cost savings from its work with energy technology partner LoweConex.
It is one example Pickering points to when explaining how environmental investment can help address the pressures facing retailers, rather than simply adding to them.
“Sustainability isn’t an optional extra for us, it is central to our purpose and our values,” he stresses.
“Crucially, we also see operating more sustainably as a way to help manage some of the external pressures that face retailers across the board.”
Following OurCoop’s Sustainable Retailer of the Year win at the RG Excellence Awards 2026, Pickering sets out an approach built around renewable energy, efficiency and partnerships, with benefits intended to reach beyond the business itself.
The society was created in January 2026 through the combination of Central Co-op, The Midcounties Co-operative and Chelmsford Star Co-op. Pickering says bringing the businesses together as the UK’s largest independent co-operative society gives it greater scope to expand its impact.
Making the energy investment pay
Energy independence is central to that ambition. OurCoop has installed solar panels at more than 130 sites, generating around 4.7 GWh of renewable electricity over the past year and saving more than 800 tonnes of CO₂, according to Pickering.
Renewable energy from its offshore wind and solar partnerships now provides the equivalent of around 22 per cent of its electricity needs.
Pickering explains: “As a Member-owned business, we’re here to create long-term value for our Members and communities. Running a successful Society and protecting the places we serve go hand in hand.”
Alongside generation, the business is targeting the energy consumed by its stores. Its partnership with LoweConex has automated heating and refrigeration controls across a range of FoodCoop shops.
Pickering says this has reduced energy use by 2.5 GWh and emissions by more than 400 tonnes of CO₂ since 2024, while improving temperature management and maintenance efficiency.
“Those are practical benefits for the Society as well as the environment,” he adds.
The calculation extends beyond immediate savings. Generating electricity and securing long-term supply agreements also help the society plan for its future energy requirements and reduce exposure to price fluctuations.
Using collective scale
That longer-term approach is also shaping how OurCoop works with other co-operatives. The society led a renewable electricity agreement linked to the London Array offshore wind farm on behalf of five independent co-operatives.
The agreement provides up to 53 GWh of green electricity a year, enough to power more than 400 premises, including retail stores, funeral homes and travel agents.
“It’s another practical example of the difference we can make when co-operatives work together, sharing their collective scale and expertise to achieve a common goal,” Pickering notes.
Through Younity, its joint venture with Octopus Energy, OurCoop also supports nearly 100 community energy organisations. That support includes power purchase agreements, financial and practical assistance, and connections with volunteers.
“We’re helping communities generate and own clean energy themselves,” he says. “It’s a great example of co-operation in action, giving local people greater control over where their energy comes from and how it’s generated.”
Tackling food waste on the shop floor
Food redistribution is another strand of the strategy. OurCoop works with Olio and Too Good to Go to prevent waste and put surplus food to use locally.
Since its Olio partnership began in 2024, the society has redistributed 5.4 million food items, equivalent to around four million meals.
“That’s a significant contribution to tackling food waste and supporting people in our communities,” Pickering notes.
He argues that partnerships work best when colleagues have the tools to take part. Smart-meter dashboards, energy-saving guidance and colleague competitions help store teams understand their contribution, while regular supplier sessions support discussions about supply-chain environmental impacts and changes.
“Our aim is to give people the information, tools and support they need, then share what works across our family of businesses,” he says.
“By bringing people together and learning from one another, we can achieve much more than we could individually.”
Sharing the ambition
Pickering wants sustainability to run through the wider customer offer, rather than operate as a separate programme. He points to Fairtrade products in FoodCoop stores, environmental learning in Little Pioneers nurseries and EnergyCoop’s Community Power Tariff, which offers electricity from 100 per cent community-owned renewable generation.
“It’s important that sustainability is part of everything we do, rather than something that sits separately from our wider business strategy,” he says.
With more than one million members, OurCoop sees an opportunity to involve more people in that work. Its shops can demonstrate sustainability in practice, while Younity’s volunteering platform connects people with local community energy groups seeking time and skills to develop renewable projects.
The next phase will include expanding renewable generation, reducing food waste, improving water efficiency and supporting biodiversity. Pickering’s emphasis, however, is as much on how the society delivers these priorities as on the initiatives themselves.
“The biggest lesson is that making a lasting difference takes more than investment alone,” he says. “It’s about measuring our progress, involving our colleagues and building strong, long-term partnerships with people who share our ambition.”

items.title: The place where Britons are most likely to use loyalty cards... and how much they earn each year
items.summary: Shoppers have been persuaded to join by 'member prices' - discounts that are only available to those who have signed up to their points scheme.
items.body:
The place where Britons are most likely to use loyalty cards... and how much they earn each year
From Nectar to Clubcard and Boots Advantage Card to Avios, many of us use loyalty cards to earn points on our shopping.
The number of people signed up to them has increased in recent years, starting in the cost-of-living crisis when the price of everyday goods started to climb.
Shoppers have also been persuaded to join by 'member prices' - discounts that are only available to those who have signed up to their points scheme.
But where in Britain are the biggest fans of loyalty cards? New research has revealed which parts of the country are keenest to collect points - and how much they earn each year.
According to American Express, those in the south west of England are the most likely to belong to a loyalty scheme, with 96 per cent already earning rewards.
They said they earned rewards on more than a third (35 per cent) of all their shopping.
London and the east of England also make their spending count, with 94 per cent earning rewards on their everyday shop.
People in the West Midlands are least likely to earn points through a loyalty scheme at just 77 per cent.
Shoppers in Northern Ireland have lower take-up, with 84 per cent belonging to at least one loyalty scheme.
However, they made the biggest savings, netting a total of £158.40 in points, perks or vouchers in the past 12 months.
This was despite only being signed up to eight rewards schemes on average, far lower than shoppers in other areas.
People in London were signed up to twice as many loyalty schemes - an average of 17 each and the most of any region of Britain.
They saved an average of £152.80 per year by using them.
Yorkshire and Humberside was in third place with an annual saving of £145.90. People there typically had 12 loyalty cards.
American Express found that loyalty scheme members saved an estimated total of £4.43billion by redeeming rewards over the past year.

Three in five (59 per cent) of rewards programme members got additional perks and benefits through their programmes such as travel upgrades, access to exclusive events, airport lounges or members-only areas.
This is Money has previously reported on what different loyalty schemes have on offer and what shoppers around the UK think of them.
Caroline Bouvet, vice president of products and partnerships at American Express, said: ‘Rewards have become much more than an occasional perk – they are now a way for consumers to get more value from their everyday spending.
‘While consumers’ approach to rewards varies by region, it is clear they are using rewards to get more value from the money they're already spending, whether that's helping to reduce the cost of the weekly shop or saving towards a holiday.'

items.title: Snag is making AI work. Its CTO thinks retailers need a reality check
items.summary: In a three-part video series from Patchworks, Snag CTO Tom Martin discusses where AI has earned its place in the business, and why he remains sceptical of some of its promises…   Preparing a product launch across six online stores used to take a day of Tom Martin’s week. With AI helping the team work...
items.body:
In a three-part video series from Patchworks, Snag CTO Tom Martin discusses where AI has earned its place in the business, and why he remains sceptical of some of its promises…
Preparing a product launch across six online stores used to take a day of Tom Martin’s week. With AI helping the team work across its connected systems, that same prep now takes minutes.
It’s the sort of result that makes retail leaders pay attention, although Martin, tights retailer Snag’s co-founder and CTO, is just as willing to discuss the expense and effort involved in achieving it. Having changed how his own business operates, he has little patience for the more extravagant promises made on the technology’s behalf.
“I’ve never seen a technology that is more overhyped and at the same time more transformational,” he says.
Snag’s experience helps explain that assessment. It’s used AI and connected systems to update more than 14,000 products in a single operation, yet it has neither cut jobs nor found that adopting the technology automatically means spending less.
In AI in retail: what actually works, Martin joins Patchworks CEO Jim Herbert for three video conversations about those experiences, with Retail Gazette content director Kieran Howells hosting the final episode. Together, they examine the decisions behind Snag’s results and what other retailers should consider before committing their own budgets.
Getting the systems talking
Serving customers in more than 100 countries through six Shopify storefronts and five warehouse management systems, Snag has plenty of experience of the administrative burden that accompanies growth.
The company has never operated its own servers or employed in-house developers, leaving its technical team to contend with a collection of software services that needed to exchange product and order information. Keeping that information moving absorbed time that could otherwise have gone into developing the business.
For retailers whose launch schedules still depend on someone working through several applications, the problem will sound familiar. Having the products and commercial plans ready counts for little if preparing the systems takes another day.
Patchworks connects Snag’s commerce and operational systems, while AI gives its team a different way to work with them. Martin explains how requests made in plain English become instructions those systems can carry out, alongside the difficulties Snag encountered when putting that approach into practice.
His account gives retailers considering similar projects a closer look at the work involved, particularly where access restrictions or inconsistent data complicate an apparently straightforward request.
Making the numbers work
The financial discussion is equally candid, with Herbert describing the unexpected bills some teams have faced after taking AI agents into production.
“It’s not cost-out for us; it’s cost-shifting,” says Martin, whose experience challenges the assumption that faster processes necessarily come cheaper.
The episodes explore why the way a task is performed can substantially affect its running costs, especially when repeated across a large catalogue. Martin also discusses where Snag chooses not to use AI and what happens to a team’s workload when familiar bottlenecks disappear.
The trio brings those questions into the management discussion in the final episode, examining accountability and the pressure retailers feel to keep up. For leaders weighing their next investment, the series offers a chance to hear how an operational retailer has approached decisions they may soon face themselves.
Watch the three-part series and explore AI in retail: what actually works.

items.title: Greggs taps Auror technology across stores as prolific shoplifter avoids jail
items.summary: Greggs reports that it is rolling out Auror crime reporting and intelligence technology across its stores amid a rise in shoplifting.The British bakery and fast food chain made the announcement as a shoplifter who stole more than £2,000 worth of soft drinks from a single Greggs store returned to the
items.body:
Greggs reports that it is rolling out Auror crime reporting and intelligence technology across its stores amid a rise in shoplifting.
The British bakery and fast food chain made the announcement as a shoplifter who stole more than £2,000 worth of soft drinks from a single Greggs store returned to the community after being handed a suspended sentence.
Since May, Tiffany O'Neill, 28, has been arrested, charged and remanded to court 11 times. She was ultimately charged with 69 theft offences.
Yet when she appeared for sentencing at Croydon Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, having pleaded guilty to a total of 80 offences, she avoided being sent to prison and was handed a 26 week sentence, suspended for 12 months.
New constraints on magistrates and judges that came into force earlier this year require a sentence of less than a year to be suspended unless very specific exceptions apply.
The Met said it was highlighting this case to reiterate its calls for the criminal justice system to hold prolific offenders to account. It is estimated that officers have spent more than 120 hours on this single case since O’Neill’s arrest in May, including preparing case files, carrying out further arrests and attending court hearings. At all but one court appearance in recent months she was granted bail, despite repeatedly breaching her bail conditions and returning to target the same Greggs store on Electric Avenue in Brixton.
O’Neill was initially banned from entering the London Borough of Lambeth and required to wear a GPS tag as a condition of her bail. However, despite repeated offending whilst on bail, the GPS tag was never fitted.
Three sentencing hearings were previously adjourned because she failed to appear in court, and a fourth was delayed earlier this week due to tech issues at the court. In addition to the suspended sentence, a Criminal Behaviour Order was also granted banning her from Brixton town centre and all Greggs stores in the UK for two years.
Sergeant Chris Wilkinson, who led the investigation, says: “Our officers worked relentlessly over several months to build the evidence needed to bring this prolific offender before the courts."
“Despite multiple arrests and repeated offences, we remained focused on securing a positive outcome for our community. Her persistent offending caused repeated distress to staff, harmed the business and placed a significant demand on police resources."
He adds: “We recognise that courts are obliged to follow the guidelines on suspending sentences, but it’s obviously a disappointment that someone who we know has reoffended so frequently is now back out in the community. We hope this marks a change in her offending, but if it doesn’t we will be there to intervene and put her back before the courts.”
Roisin Currie, Chief Executive at Greggs, comments: “The safety and wellbeing of our colleagues and customers is always our priority, and persistent incidents of theft can have a real impact on those in our shops. We are grateful to the Metropolitan Police for their continued work with retailers, including Greggs, to tackle repeat offending."
“Retail crime is an industry wide issue and we continue to strengthen our approach, including the roll-out of Auror technology across all of our shops, investment in CCTV and trials of a new shop format in a small number of locations exposed to higher levels of anti-social behaviour. We also work closely with law enforcement and industry partners to share intelligence, helping us to better prevent and respond to these incidents and maintain safe, welcoming environments for our colleagues and customers."
“We support efforts to apprehend repeat offenders, and we welcome calls for meaningful consequences for those who repeatedly target retailers. Importantly, we would like to see a renewed focus on positive interventions and services that prevent reoffending.”

items.body:
Retail Technology Show has announced the first members of the advisory board for its 2027 event, which will take place at London Excel on 21st-22nd April.
These are: Alfie Meekings, Chief Transformation and Technology Officer, AllSaints; Constanze Freienstein, Managing Director, Peek & Cloppenburg* Düsseldorf; and Mohsen Ghasempour, Chief AI & Technology Officer, Morrisons.
In a LinkedIn post, Retail Technology Show said: "Our advisory board brings first-hand experience, fresh perspectives and a clear understanding of retail’s biggest priorities. Their input helps shape RTS around the challenges retailers are tackling and the opportunities they want to explore, ensuring the show delivers relevant insights, practical ideas and inspiration."
It added: "A show for retailers, shaped by retailers. Join us in welcoming them to the RTS community, and keep an eye out for our next advisory board announcement!"
RTIH at RTS 2027
RTIH will be out in force at Retail Technology Show 2027. Visitors to our stand will be able to pick up a free copy of issue 12 of our printed magazine.
This year's issue (number 10) was our biggest and best yet, clocking in at over 100 pages. Check it out here.
To get your company in the magazine and reach thousands of retail technology decision-makers via promotional article and full page advertisement opportunities, drop us a line here.
Mohsen Ghasempour
In September, Morrisons appointed Mohsen Ghasempour as Chief AI Officer, a newly created role that will see him establish a central data science and AI function for the UK grocery retailer. He joined from Kingfisher, where he had served as Chief AI Officer since March 2024 following more than two years as Group AI Director.
He takes overall responsibility for data and AI strategy, with a remit spanning customer growth, colleague empowerment, operational efficiency, manufacturing excellence and commercial excellence. He reports directly to Morrisons CEO Rami Baitiéh and took up the role on 1st October.
“Creation of this new role reflects our commitment to ensuring Morrisons is embracing the opportunities in data and AI at pace, with focus and in the right way,” said Baitiéh.
“Mohsen is a recognised expert in the field with hands on experience of unlocking the potential of technology to deliver innovative new solutions that serve customers, empower colleagues and deliver measurable business impact.”
Ghasempour said: “I’m excited about joining Morrisons and building the team that will help the business make effective and responsible use of AI in the years ahead, to deliver real benefits for customers and colleagues.”

items.title: Michelle Kay Powell takes on Data and Analytics Digital Transformation Lead role at Primark

Her CV also includes stints at Virgin Media O2 and Telegraph Media Group.Kal
items.body:
Michelle Kay Powell is starting a new position as Data and Analytics Digital Transformation Lead at Primark.
She joins from Infosys Consulting where she served as Senior Consultant, CX, CRM, Customer & AI Transformation. Her CV also includes stints at Virgin Media O2 and Telegraph Media Group.
Kallikor
Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.
The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation.
By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, the retailer says it can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, Director of Supply Chain at Primark, says: “As we continue to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical."
"A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations - from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations - before we commit capital spend."
"This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well-informed decisions as we evolve our network.”
By modelling operational flows in detail - from pick paths and labour constraints to throughput variability and service impacts - Primark can see how proposed changes will perform in practice before they are introduced. The models are built from its operational data, with the aim of ensuring outcomes reflect how the system actually performs under a range of real operating conditions rather than relying on assumptions or averaged views of the network.
The modelling also establishes a living decision environment built on Primark’s operational data that can be reused and extended as new strategic questions arise. Rather than commissioning a new analysis for each decision, teams can continuously test alternatives within the same validated model as the supply chain evolves.
Through simulation and AI enabled scenario exploration, they can run and compare multiple operating futures side-by-side, assessing trade offs across cost, service, capacity and risk in parallel.
Jack O’Connell, CEO and Co-Founder at Kallikor, says: “At Primark’s scale, no supply chain decision exists in isolation. A change in one distribution centre can affect capacity, flow, service and performance across the wider network. Our role is to help teams explore decisions that would otherwise carry too much uncertainty, testing different scenarios before implementation so leaders can understand the trade-offs and move forward with confidence."
"We’re proud to support Primark as they build a simulation led decision-making capability, beginning with their distribution centres and creating the foundations for better decisions across the wider supply chain over time.”
While the initial focus is on distribution centre configuration, the modelling environment is designed to be reused as new questions arise, allowing teams to test automation pathways, capital investments, network design changes and future growth scenarios within the same validated system.

items.title: Ikea announces AI powered home furnishing pilot with German real estate platform ImmoScout24
items.summary: A new Ikea pilot in Germany is tapping AI to help people turn images of empty rooms in property listings into inspiring spaces featuring real products.  The retailer says that the pilot with Germany’s largest real estate platform, ImmoScout24, also gives it an opportunity to explore the re
items.body:
A new Ikea pilot in Germany is tapping AI to help people turn images of empty rooms in property listings into inspiring spaces featuring real products.
The retailer says that the pilot with Germany’s largest real estate platform, ImmoScout24, also gives it an opportunity to explore the real estate sector from a different perspective, better understand people’s needs and behaviours when searching for a new home, and discover new ways to connect with customers at an earlier stage.
Developed by the Ikea global digital teams, the solution analyses images of empty and furnished rooms and creates realistic visualisations featuring Ikea furniture and home accessories, with product selections developed together with interior design experts. The pilot currently covers living rooms and bedrooms, with the possibility of expanding into other rooms as the solution develops.
Parag Parekh, Global Chief Digital Officer (CDO) at Ikea Retail (Ingka Group), says: "The pilot represents another step in exploring how digital technologies can make home furnishing more convenient as well as fun and inspiring. It is also part of our wider ambition to create a seamless omnichannel experience, connecting the different moments when people discover, explore and shop for home furnishing solutions.”
He adds: “Depending on the learnings and outcomes of the one-year pilot, Ikea will explore opportunities to further develop and potentially expand the solution, always with the aim of creating simpler, more inspiring and accessible experiences for the many."

items.body:
GXO Logistics has announced a nine-year contract renewal with Asos, extending a partnership that began in 2013.
Over the past 13 years, GXO has worked with Asos to support the retailer's evolving business needs at its automated logistics hub in Barnsley. The renewed agreement covers warehouse fulfilment and transportation services.
"Our partnership is built on a shared commitment to delivering outstanding service and value,” says Russell Atkinson, Managing Director of Fashion, GXO UK&I. “For more than a decade we've worked together to support millions of customer orders through a highly efficient, resilient and increasingly technology enabled operation."
"Over the course of our partnership, we've been on a continuous improvement journey, helping to evolve one of the UK's most advanced e-commerce fulfilment operations. By combining the expertise of our colleagues with technology and automation, we've continued to adapt to changing customer expectations and support Asos' growth. This renewal is a testament to the strength of our relationship and the dedication of our teams, and we're excited to continue building on that success over the next nine years."
Jonny O’Hara, Logistics Director at Asos, says: “Our ambition is to be The Stylist for our customers, bringing the latest trends and exciting brands through curated, personalised experiences that help customers put together outfits with confidence."
"Delivering that experience relies on strong, flexible and reliable operations, and GXO, as leaders in the industry, have been a trusted partner for more than 13 years. As we extend our partnership for the years ahead, this renewal will support our growth while helping us continue to deliver the excellent service our customers expect.”

items.body:
UK parcel delivery company DPD is set to deploy a further 381 electric vans as part of its plan for an expected record peak period.
The new Ford E-Transits will all be on the road by mid-November. The order follows on from the delivery of 341 new Mercedes-Benz eSprinter vans in September.
In 2025 DPD delivered over 85 million parcels on electric vehicles including a predominantly diesel free final mile service within the North and South Circular in London.
Olly Craughan, DPD’s Head of Sustainability and Social Purpose, comments: “Ford is a strong partner for DPD, and we already operate a significant number of E-Transits. They have performed well for us over the last four years, while the TrustFord mobile service network also played a big part in us choosing Ford again. The enhanced range means we can now get more of these larger electric vans out on our longer routes, making a bigger difference in terms of reducing emissions."
He adds: “This is set to be our biggest peak yet, so it is great to be able to say to customers that we will have more electric vans delivering on the road than ever before. We know this is a key issue for many shippers, large and small and we are delighted to be delivering more of their parcels on electric vehicles.”
