items.title: Comment: why trade buyers still pick up the phone even after a six-figure ecommerce launch
items.summary: B2B ecommerce expert Chris Gee from Rixxo explains why phone and email are still the ‘go-to’ for many trade buyers, and what it takes for manufacturers and distributors to change those habits. A retailer is placing a repeat order with a supplier. Most of the products are in the online basket, but one line needs...
items.body:
B2B ecommerce expert Chris Gee from Rixxo explains why phone and email are still the ‘go-to’ for many trade buyers, and what it takes for manufacturers and distributors to change those habits.
A retailer is placing a repeat order with a supplier. Most of the products are in the online basket, but one line needs to go to a different branch and the buyer wants to know whether it will arrive before the weekend. A call to the rep settles both questions and gets the whole order placed. The next time, the buyer calls first.
That decision helps explain why manufacturers and distributors can spend six figures on an ecommerce platform and still have an order desk full of people taking calls and rekeying emails.
Research by Forrester Consulting, commissioned by Sana Commerce, found that seven in ten B2B organisations say their buyers bypass digital channels at critical points in the purchasing process, such as confirming prices or checking stock.
As Chris Gee, founder of digital consultancy Rixxo, puts it, “you can build a perfectly good path and still find everyone walking across the grass. These are called desire paths.” For a retail buyer juggling deliveries, replenishment and stock across several sites, the shortcut is often the person who already knows how the account works.
What the order desk does that the portal cannot
Placing an order can be the easy part. A buyer might need to hold dispatch until month-end, split a shipment between two sites, or pay partly by card when they are close to their credit limit. On the phone, those details can be settled in the same conversation. If the website handles the basket but the buyer still has to call to sort out delivery or payment, it adds a step to a job the rep could have completed in one go.
The problem can start before a platform is even bought. “The decisions were made before the problem was understood,” says Gee. “A supplier can sit through an impressive demo and come away sold on features without having worked out which jobs buyers still rely on the order desk to do. That’s how a portal can look good at launch and still send buyers back to the phone when they need to split a delivery or use their agreed payment terms.”
That’s the thinking behind Rixxo’s SPIN APE® framework for platform selection. A morning with the order desk can reveal which orders regularly end with someone saying ‘leave it with me’. Those are the orders to take into a demo. Ask vendors to show how their platform would handle them using your own pricing, credit and delivery rules. You’ll see which jobs the software can take on and where your team would still need to step in.
There is also a case for starting with orders the portal already handles well. A retailer who can reorder last month’s stock in a few clicks, build a basket over several days or order after the office closes has a reason to give it a go. More complicated orders can still go through the team while the supplier learns what keeps them there.
Why both sides keep coming back to the phone
Moving an order online saves the supplier from keying it in, but the buyer may see little benefit in doing that work themselves. One European distributor operating across six markets gave buyers a delivery advantage for ordering online. When a customer called, the rep could explain the benefit and send a basket ready to complete.
A UK parts distributor Rixxo works with took a different approach, setting a £200 minimum for phone and email orders and a £75 minimum online. For a retailer topping up a few lines, the lower threshold can make the portal the more practical option.
Those incentives carry more weight when the buyer can complete a real order without having to chase anyone. A rep who knows the account can help the buyer through that first purchase, using a live basket or a quote that links directly to checkout. The next order shows whether the buyer can do it independently, and where they still need help.
The rep’s own incentives matter just as much. If an order placed through the portal earns them less commission than one taken over the phone, it makes sense for them to keep taking calls. Giving reps credit for orders across their accounts, whichever channel the buyer uses, makes it easier for them to introduce customers to the portal. It also gives them a reason to help resolve pricing or account issues that might otherwise send the buyer straight back to email.
Where the return on investment shows up
A distributor with a £16 million turnover aimed to increase online orders from around 6% to 20% so it could grow without a matching rise in overheads. The test was how much staff time each order still took.
At another business, 1,000 six-minute phone orders took 100 hours a month. If staff still have to correct prices or confirm dispatch dates after orders move online, some of that work simply shifts. When the portal handles those details, staff can spend more time advising customers and growing accounts.
The return also depends on which orders move. A regular replenishment order and a split delivery with special terms take different amounts of effort to handle, so an average across all accounts can hide where the gains are coming from. Comparing similar orders before and after the switch gives a clearer picture of the time recovered and whether it justifies the cost of running the portal and getting buyers onto it.
“When businesses come to us for help choosing an ecommerce platform, we start by looking at how they take orders today, what their customers need and what will have to change for the people who support them,” says Gee. “That gives us a brief to take to vendors and helps us see where the business itself needs to change, whether that’s how orders are handled or how sales teams are rewarded. The test comes after launch, when a buyer has another order to place and going online is the easiest way to get the whole job done.”

items.title: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
items.summary: Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal. The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning. Continue reading...
items.body:
MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.
The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.
The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.
The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.
Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading.
Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.
The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.
 
He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’.
 
“Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas.
 
“Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”
 
The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.
Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it has only enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.
Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.
The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.
Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.
Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.
Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.
A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.
Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

items.title: ASOS introduces first dedicated Christmas partywear and gifting campaign
items.summary: ASOS has brought together comedian Ziwe, actor Harry Collett, beauty entrepreneur Toni Brattin and influencer Olivia Neill for its 2026 Christmas campaign. The retro-inspired Hotline hero film is designed to combine fashion, entertainment and expert style advice to help customers find the right look or gift for the festive season. Vanessa Spence, EVP brand & creative at...
items.body:
ASOS has brought together comedian Ziwe, actor Harry Collett, beauty entrepreneur Toni Brattin and influencer Olivia Neill for its 2026 Christmas campaign.
The retro-inspired Hotline hero film is designed to combine fashion, entertainment and expert style advice to help customers find the right look or gift for the festive season.
Vanessa Spence, EVP brand & creative at ASOS, said: “Winter is full of moments when you want to look and feel your best, whether that’s a big night out, finding the perfect gift or simply trying something new.
“With ASOS Hotline, we’re bringing together fashion, entertainment and expert styling to help our customers navigate those moments with confidence. It’s a really fun expression of our ambition to make ASOS everyone’s personal stylist, helping people find their style and make every moment their own.”
Styled by ASOS Stylist in Residence Law Roach, the campaign sees Ziwe and ASOS Marketing Insider Farron Clark field calls from Harry Collett, Toni Brattin, and Olivia Neill, each with a style dilemma.
Harry needs an outfit to meet the parents for a date that’s not quite official. Toni is heading to London for a big event and needs a look to match. While, Olivia is searching for a gift for her sister, who’s impossible to buy for.
Launched on 11 November across digital, social and editorial, the campaign is backed by a curated winter fashion edit, giving customers the wardrobe to solve their own seasonal style dilemmas. Spanning ASOS DESIGN, ARRANGE, Topshop and partner brands including Levi’s, Mango and Polo Ralph Lauren.
Law Roach, ASOS Stylist in Residence, added: “I’ve always believed in the power of fashion to give you confidence in how you show up. We all have those moments when we’re getting ready and just don’t know what to wear. To have the opportunity to help people work through those style dilemmas and find something that makes them feel good, that’s incredibly rewarding.”
The campaign was created in partnership with creative agency Baron & Baron, photographed by Nicolas Kantor, and brought to life on film by Talia Collis and Peter Bishop.

items.title: MMG expands retail media proposition across 1,700 convenience stores
items.summary: Morrisons Media Group (MMG) is growing its retail media proposition to include Morrisons’ approximately 1,700 convenience stores, giving brands and suppliers a more joined-up approach to planning campaigns across the…
items.body:
MMG expands retail media proposition across 1,700 convenience stores
Morrisons Media Group (MMG) is growing its retail media proposition to include Morrisons’ approximately 1,700 convenience stores, giving brands and suppliers a more joined-up approach to planning campaigns across the retailer’s supermarket and convenience estates.
MMG stressed the expansion comes as the UK convenience market is forecast to grow from £49.2bn in 2025 to £56.2bn by 2030, according to IGD.
Shopper behaviour is evolving too, with Lumina Intelligence reporting a 5 per cent year-on-year increase in convenience shopping visits, alongside a 7 per cent decline in items purchased per trip. These changing habits highlight the importance of tailoring campaigns to distinct shopping missions, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach across retail environments.
The expansion brings convenience media into MMG’s wider proposition, providing suppliers with a consistent point of contact and access to the group’s strategic planning, client service and proposition-development expertise.
With convenience shopping driven by different customer needs, locations and purchasing occasions, MMG will take a tailored approach to the channel, helping suppliers develop campaigns that reflect the distinct shopping behaviours of convenience customers while connecting activity to their broader retail media strategies.

Steve Newbould, head of commercial data & media, Morrisons Media Group, said: “Expanding Morrisons Media Group’s proposition into convenience is an important step in how we support our supplier partners.
“Our customers shop across different formats for different reasons, and bringing these opportunities together allows us to offer brands a more comprehensive way to engage with them. This is about building on the strength of our existing retail media proposition while recognising the growing importance of convenience.”
“The expanded proposition combines Morrisons’ retail expertise and first-party customer insights with SMG’s retail media capabilities. Suppliers will benefit from MMG’s existing strategic support, including insights informed by Morrisons’ first-party data ecosystem, MoreViu, to help shape campaign planning around relevant customer missions and commercial objectives.”

items.title: Aldi cuts head office jobs in shake-up of UK operations
items.summary: Aldi is planning to cut up to 150 jobs from its UK head office as part of the discount grocer’s ongoing shake-up of its tech and admin operations. The supermarket chain is consulting on the loss of up to 150 roles in its technology team, after cutting 103 jobs from its finance and administration department [...]
items.body:
Aldi cuts head office jobs in shake-up of UK operations
Aldi is planning to cut up to 150 jobs from its UK head office as part of the discount grocer’s ongoing shake-up of its tech and admin operations.
The supermarket chain is consulting on the loss of up to 150 roles in its technology team, after cutting 103 jobs from its finance and administration department earlier this year. It has also made nearly 20 buying directors redundant.
The job cuts come as Aldi seeks to reach 1,500 stores in the UK, as the grocer and rival Lidl put pressure on competitors Asda and Morrisons, who have each been battling with significant debt piles since being taken over by private equity.
Aldi’s German-based owners are cutting back on the number of head office roles in each of its country operations, which include the US, Australia and China, as it centralises more admin and tech functions.
The group is outsourcing its finance, procurement and administration jobs to India, the Guardian has reported, through its partnership with Genpact, a New York-headquartered firm which uses AI to streamline business functions.
Aldi’s consultation on its redundancies is set to begin in the coming months, it is understood. The company has cut the number of hours worked by the agency staff who clean its Warwickshire headquarters, the Guardian reported.
Aldi loses ground to rivals
The German discounter has grown rapidly in recent years, putting pressure on even the biggest UK supermarket chains, like Tesco and Sainsbury’s, which have responded with Aldi price-match ranges.
But Aldi’s growth has slowed in recent months, with the company growing its takings by just 0.4 per cent in the 12 weeks to November, according to the latest figures from Worldpanel by Numerator.
This is lower than the 6.6 per cent sales growth achieved by its rival Lidl, and the 1.2 and 0.8 per cent notched by Tesco and Sainsbury’s. Aldi’s market share was 10.4 per cent in the lead-up to November, lower than 10.5 per cent at the same time last year.
In September, Aldi set out plans to invest £900m in opening 40 new stores in the coming year. It currently operates 1,092 shops in the UK but wants to reach 1,500.
A spokesperson for the supermarket chain said: “At Aldi, our promise to customers is that we will always offer great quality products at unbeatable prices. Across our international business, we continuously review all aspects of our operations to ensure we operate simply, efficiently and use our global scale to deliver on that promise.
“We are therefore making some adjustments to the way parts of our UK business are structured. Any changes are being introduced gradually and following a consultation period. We recognise that this is difficult for those involved, so we are giving colleagues as much notice as possible, with full support available to everyone affected.”

items.title: Mini record player on track for No 1 in Christmas toy parade
items.summary: Industry experts pick out tiny turntable as one of their ‘15 hottest toys’ for the festive season A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn. The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season. Continue reading...
items.body:
A record player so small it belongs at a party in a Barbie Dreamhouse is one of this year’s must-have Christmas gifts as the vinyl revival takes an unexpected turn.
The £19.99 micro music set plays dinky 1.5in records and comes with an exclusive “mini vinyl” of the school disco favourite APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars. The toy makes the Toy Retailers Association’s annual DreamToys list of the 15 “hottest toys” this festive season.
The Mini Brands record player taps into the huge market for collectible toys. Part of the appeal is the 45 mini records to collect, ranging from Billie Eilish’s Birds of a Feather to Neil Diamond’s Sweet Caroline. The discs are sold separately in £8 “blind balls” with part of the attraction being the mystery of which songs are inside.
The trend for miniature products comes because making something smaller “makes it feel cuter”, suggests Melissa Symonds, executive director of UK toys at market research company Circana. While adults enjoyed the novelty, she suggested that children would relish acting out playing records in the same way that their parents did.
The record player is unlikely to satisfy high-end audiophiles, however, because the “vinyl” isn’t real. Instead, the discs contain a chip that activates a 30-second clip from the player’s internal memory.
The rundown of must-have toys comes as retailers brace for their most important trading period: the final three months of the year typically account for 45% of annual toy sales.
Hopes are high after sales jumped 13% to £2.6bn in the first nine months, according to Circana, which it said was the “fastest growth in a decade”. During that period, 257m toys were sold – 38m more than in the same period last year.
The buoyant picture is partly due to the “squishies” craze. Retailers are racing to keep up with demand for the sensory toys with NeeDoh the most popular official brand.
Paul Reader, chair of the DreamToys selection panel at the Toy Retailers Association, said 2026 had been “incredible for the UK toy market”.
He added: “We haven’t seen anything like squishies since the days of fidget spinners and before that POGs [a milk cap game].” Children loved the tactile toys, he said, because once you’ve “got it in your hands … you just can’t put it down”.
After a period when “kidults” (aged 12 and over) buying expensive Lego sets and collectible figurines propped up toy sales, Reader said demand for toys like squishies was pulling children back into toy shops. “We’re seeing more children coming into stores, that after-school time is busier.”
The 15 toys on the Dreamtoys list range in price from £13.99 for a NeeDoh squishy to £129.99 for a dinosaur-themed Hot Wheels garage. The furReal Gabby the Grow & Roar Tiger – an interactive cuddly toy that transforms from a cub into a tiger – may thrill an animal lover. For the legions of K-pop Demon Hunter fans there is a singing doll that belts out their hit Golden.
The near-£50 Pokémon 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box also makes the list, but as fans queue up outside stores to buy the latest card releases parents are advised not to leave tracking this gift down until the last minute.

items.title: Christmas adverts 2026 reviewed: From John Lewis to M&S’s hot Santa
items.summary: Blimey. The dog’s just emerging nervously from behind the sofa and the smell of gunpowder still hangs over countless fields and gardens. But here comes the full-on commercial glorification of Christ’s birth. Bring it on. As ever, its arrival is heralded by ‘the Christmas ads’. As much a part of the traditional celebration as a [...]
items.body:
Christmas adverts 2026 reviewed: From John Lewis to M&S’s hot Santa
Blimey. The dog’s just emerging nervously from behind the sofa and the smell of gunpowder still hangs over countless fields and gardens. But here comes the full-on commercial glorification of Christ’s birth. Bring it on. As ever, its arrival is heralded by ‘the Christmas ads’. As much a part of the traditional celebration as a variety box and a pig in a blanket, it’s the one time of year that you, the glorious British public, actually pay attention to the stuff we make in the advertising business.
The rest of the year you happily pay a premium to block us out… I guess that’s the Christmas spirit working, as you welcome us and our messages into your homes.
We’re going to have a look at some of them and see if it’s a vintage year. I thought it would be interesting to understand what advertising people made of them but – more importantly – what real people think about them: are they on song or tone deaf?
One hell of a year
And we should also bear in mind the context, because while it is indeed the season to be jolly, it’s also been one hell of a year, with sky-rocketing interest rates, the eye-watering cost of living and wars raging in Europe and the Middle East.
Are we just hoping for a hand-crank radio and a multi-pack of baked beans in our stockings or do we still crave a little more?
John Lewis Christmas advert 2026: Gloria and Pickles
The John Lewis ad is, in so many ways, an institution now. And again the craft here (including the soundtrack, casting and direction) is flawless. This year’s ad, which stars Kristin Scott Thomas and a shonky wooden dog called Pickles, scored 5.6 stars according to System1, a business that measures the effectiveness of ads. They say it’s John Lewis’s strongest one since Excitable Edgar in 2019. But there is an argument raging around it: a lot of other voices in the business point out that, while it’s good fun, it suffers from a lack of emotional engagement. There’s no tear-jerking twist. It’s supposed to say a personal gift beats cash, but it comes across as implying “spending money is the only way to win the kids’ affection”.
Piers Morgan called it “the worst advert I’ve ever seen for anything”. Sarah Vine dubbed the grandkids “spoiled, entitled, rude and overindulged.” The Spectator branded it “lamentably bad”. And it’s getting 77 per cent negative social sentiment from the public. For me, if grandma tarted up a room to look like a disco for my Christmas present, I’d feel a little cheated… but maybe I’m just as entitled as the kids in the ad.
M&S Christmas advert 2026: Hot Santa takes the lead
Next there’s M&S. I must declare an interest here: my agency wrote the script that reunited French and Saunders a few years back. But times change… For the first time in a long time it rolls together food, fashion and home. It starts off stronger than the Christmas punch, with a PR shot of James Norton wearing only a towel. More About Advertising rated it nine out of 10, calling it “a Christmas classic.” It also backed merging the categories, because food continues to drive profits while fashion grabs headlines. Creative Review called it “glitzy but funny”. And you? Well, Vicky Pattison called it “the best advert I have ever seen” and Stacey Dooley said “Absolutely yes”.
So hot Santa seems to be landing his sled in the right spot! M&S looks like the early winner based on public mood. It has a “humour beats tears” formula and a celebrity that everyone wants to talk about. The open question is still effectiveness: hot Santa is great for reach and talkability, but the real test is whether it translates to sales…
Tesco Christmas advert 2026: The delivery drivers say breaks every rule
Tesco is the only other Christmas ad being talked about so far… and not for the right reasons. Lizzie (Anna Maxwell Martin) sends her Tesco Christmas order to her old address, hundreds of miles away. The driver turns out to be her long-lost school friend Polly (Roisin Conaty), and their road trip to deliver it ends with Polly joining the family for Christmas. A heartwarming festive tale, right?
But The Grocer (the trade rag for supermarkets) reports that Tesco delivery drivers have called it out for doing “literally everything we are specifically forbidden from doing in one short clip”. Drivers have accused Tesco of “acting like this isn’t a sackable offence”. That’s a problem when believability is so important. Although, for balance, they also voted it ahead of Sainsbury’s, Aldi, Asda and Lidl, with 35 per cent of the public calling it ‘an absolute cracker’… Let’s wait for the new year follow-up, in which Polly’s up in front of HR, shall we? I’m off to stockpile mince pies but I’ll be back next week with more.
Jon Williams is founder and chief creative officer at Freedom Works

items.body:
Dash Pink Lady Apple launches across multiple retailers
Soft drink brand Dash has secured more retail listings for the Pink Lady Apple Sparkling Water, which is set to launch nationwide across Sainsbury’s, Asda, Waitrose and Ocado.
The flavour launched six months ago is one of Tesco’s best-selling products according to the business.
The launch was part of the company’s wider innovation plans to drive growth at retailers and aims to create a soft drink which stands out in the traditional aisles fixture.
Dash also aims to meet consumer demand for healthier alternatives in the beverages category, with cleaner-label drinks, no added sugar, sweeteners or calories.
The launch is a collaboration between British-grown Pink Lady Apples, combining sparkling water with the taste of Pink Lady Apples.
The Dash Pink Lady Apple 4-packs are now available in Sainsbury’s, Asda, Waitrose and Whole Foods, with 12-packs also listed on Ocado and Amazon.
Subscribe to Grocery Gazette for free
Sign up here to get the latest grocery and food news each morning
The launch was also supported by major social media traction, with over 1m social views across Dash’s Instagram, TikTok and influencer reshares alongside multiple entries across social and email giveaways.
Alex Wright, co-founder of Dash said: “We’ve always believed that great innovation comes from challenging convention, and this launch was an opportunity to do exactly that.
“Rather than putting another drink on the soft drinks shelf and hoping shoppers would find it, we wanted to put Pink Lady Apple Sparkling Water where the ingredient itself could do the talking.
“Seeing Pink Lady Apple Sparkling Water rank third among new drink flavours in UK supermarkets, alongside launches from some of the biggest names in soft drinks, shows there is real appetite for innovation that challenges convention and finds new ways to connect with shoppers.”

As demand for the Scandinavian lifestyle continues to influence the UK retail landscape, Swedish heritage brand Tretorn is stepping up its UK retail presence by partnering with East London independent retailer Goodhood as part of its wider European expansion strategy.
With the UK identified as a priority growth market, the partnership marks an important step in introducing Tretorn’s evolving brand identity to a new generation of UK consumers. Tretorn is pursuing a wholesale-led strategy in the UK to build accessibility across retail categories, while using curated partnerships such as Goodhood to introduce its evolving premium offering to a new, design-conscious audience. Known for its curated approach to fashion, design and lifestyle, Goodhood offers a strategic platform for Tretorn to connect with a more design-conscious audience.
The collaboration will see a curated Tretorn edit arrive at Goodhood from mid-November, supported by an in-store activation on Sunday, November 15th, along with further UK retail partnerships planned for 2027.

items.title: ‘I’d steal 10-15 times a day’: ex-offenders on the addictions driving prolific shoplifting
items.summary: Former shoplifters say treatment and drug rehabilitation are essential to ending cycle of theft and imprisonment Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions. “I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.” Continue reading...
items.body:
When Rhys, 34, stole goods from shops across Birmingham, he would often leave notes for the staff apologising for his actions.
“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”
Rhys was in the grips of drug addiction and turned to shoplifting to fund his habit. He had struggled with drug use since he was a teenager and then, in 2019, he took crack cocaine for the first time. “Within a week, I was going into shops and shoplifting for it, because you just can’t get enough,” he said.
Over the next few years, he shoplifted 10-15 times a day and was sent to prison several times. However, without help to tackle his addiction, Rhys struggled to change his behaviour.
“I’d spend hours shoplifting but, at the end of the day, I still wouldn’t have anything to eat. I’d be jumping back over the fence to go through the bins to get myself a sandwich. I wouldn’t even get myself a bottle of water,” he said. “My priority was always getting the stuff to sell for drugs.”
On Wednesday, the home secretary announced plans to target 500 of the most prolific shoplifters across the country with police crackdowns in 17 areas. Measures include banning repeat offenders from high streets and town centres, closer monitoring of offenders with regular hearings before a judge and the use of electronic tagging.
But former shoplifters say many prolific thieves are in the grip of drug addiction or experiencing mental health crises, and without more funding for support services, the problem will not go away.
Keeley, 44, was once labelled Birmingham’s most prolific shoplifter, stealing between £5,000 and £9,000 worth of goods a day. She was sent to prison 28 times. Keeley had been addicted to drugs since the age of 13, after being groomed by an older man, and stole items such as designer handbags, which she could sell quickly to fund her habit. Her biggest fear was withdrawal, which had previously left her in hospital for 10 days.
She said shoplifting was an exhausting necessity – one that often led to her walking 30,000 steps a day. “Shoplifting, to a lot of us, is the closest to a victimless crime as you can get. You’re not violating anyone’s house or privacy, or robbing food out of their mouth.
“I know it’s not right, but it’s what we tell ourselves to justify it at the time – that you’re not hurting anyone – because none of us want to be doing what we’re doing.”
Keeley said she “didn’t get caught much for the amount of stuff that I stole”. Yet she spent three decades in and out of prison, never receiving the help she needed.
She eventually turned her life around when an off-duty security guard referred her to a drug support service, which led to her receiving buprenorphine injections to treat her opioid dependence.
“We’re crying that we’ve got a shoplifting crisis, and we’re crying that we’ve got a drug crisis, but no one’s doing anything about the two together,” Keeley said. “If you treat the root cause and take the addiction away, we’ve got no reason to go out and commit crime.”
For Rhys, help came in the form of an outreach navigator – a professional who connects vulnerable people to social services, housing and healthcare. He has been in recovery for 18 months, spends his time volunteering and has left shoplifting behind.
“I went into Aldi the other day, and I asked for a carrier bag and scanned it straight away. It’s such a weird comparison – now I’m scanning these 30p bags. But before, I was going in there and filling a suitcase to steal,” he said.
The social justice charity Revolving Doors said addiction, poor mental health and homelessness – often all three at once – were substantial drivers of Britain’s shoplifting epidemic.
Pavan Dhaliwal, the charity’s chief executive, said: “The anger of retailers and shop workers is justified. Theft is not victimless, and abuse of staff is intolerable.
“But if we want fewer thefts, rather than just more arrests, we have to ask a harder question: why does the same small group of people keep cycling through crisis and custody repeatedly?”
She said services that can direct people away from addiction and into stable housing were essential. “The people we work with show that recovery and rebuilding lives are possible with the right support.”
Sean, 44, has been to prison 42 times since 2000. For decades, he had not spent more than six months out of custody and felt “powerless to addiction” that drove him to crime after a traumatic childhood.
He stole food and clothes because all his money was spent on drugs, and prison brought no long-term solutions.
“The last five times I was in prison, I was a recovery mentor, taking people on circuits every day in the yard, feeling on top of my game,” Sean said. “But back in Wigan, usually within a couple of days or even a couple of hours, I’d be back doing what I’ve always done. I was completely let down by services.”
It was only when he was picked up at the prison gates by an addiction recovery service and started therapy that his life turned around. Sean now runs Rehab Fitness, which helps people recovering from addiction through group exercise and wellness activities.
He said many of his friends had turned to shop crime because there were “no consequences”, adding that the intervention should be help and support, not prison.
Prison also failed to rehabilitate Roy, 36. He was jailed several times – on one occasion after stealing wine from a shop while under the influence of drugs and alcohol.
“I had money in my pocket. I don’t know why I did it – I couldn’t even remember it afterwards. I was a different person; dead behind the eyes,” he said. “Prison would be a reset but I’d be straight in with the old crowd when I came out.”
Roy managed to get clean, and now runs Iron Minds Academy, which offers physical fitness and mentoring to young men in Wigan. “I just want to stop other young people getting to that point, for them to see there’s another path,” he said.
“When you’re leaving school, no one says I want to be on the streets addicted to heroin. We need to stop it before it gets that far, it can save someone’s life.”

items.title: Reform-linked Innovest rejoins race for Poundland ahead of MP grilling
items.summary: An Irish investment firm linked to Reform UK has re-entered the race to buy Poundland as the retail chain’s owners prepare for a showdown with MPs. Innovest, run by Irish businessman Shane Corby, had been effectively discounted from the running to buy Poundland last month, but has since provided proof of funds for its bid [...]
items.body:
Reform-linked Innovest rejoins race for Poundland ahead of MP grilling
An Irish investment firm linked to Reform UK has re-entered the race to buy Poundland as the retail chain’s owners prepare for a showdown with MPs.
Innovest, run by Irish businessman Shane Corby, had been effectively discounted from the running to buy Poundland last month, but has since provided proof of funds for its bid to buy the entire company, sources told City AM.
Innovest has reportedly received public backing from Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesperson, and is being advised by former Reform election candidate Charles Bunker.
Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owns Poundland, has refused a number of solvent bids to the retailer because it is insisting that it be paid in full for a £22.5m loan it inherited from PepCo, the group’s previous owner, when it bought the company for £1 last year.
Xyra Group, a little-known investment firm run by 23-year old Manvedeep Singh, has offered to pay £12.5m up front, while Martin Property Group, which owns National Car Parks, has offered £7.5m. The value of Innovest’s bid is not known, but it is understood its current funded offer is lower than the sum it had initially promised.
Innovest and Corby could not be reached for comment. Gordon Brothers declined to comment.
Gordon Brothers has faced significant criticism for refusing solvent offers for Poundland, with some speculating that the group is attempting to push the retailer towards collapse to allow it to strip more money from the firm.
Poundland’s owners filed a notice to appoint administrators last week, giving it until Thursday this week to secure the retailer’s future before its creditors can call in their debts.
The company’s management could apply to extend this moratorium, City AM understands. Gordon Brothers’ decision to release £10m to Poundland to allow it to pay suppliers may help the retailer avoid imminent collapse.
MPs to ‘go hard’ on Poundland owner
At around 2pm, parliamentarians on the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will grill bosses from Gordon Brothers and Poundland in separate hearings.
Gordon Brothers has come under intense scrutiny from Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee. Mark Newton-Jones, a senior managing director at the investment firm, is expected to attend the first grilling, followed by a second meeting with Poundland’s top brass.
In an unusual step for committee hearings, MPs agreed to allow sessions to take place in private due to the sensitivity of commercial information being revealed during the current 10-day moratorium that is protecting Poundland from creditor action.
Details of the meetings are expected to be disclosed when the moratorium ends on Thursday.
The committee is expected to demand answers on debt repayments owed by Poundland, the protection of jobs for some 12,000 people and whether acceptable bids have been considered by Gordon Brothers, City AM understands.
Members of the committee are also concerned about Gordon Brothers’ role in the administration process and whether it has racked up extra fees that are boosting returns for the firm.
One source close to the committee said they expected Byrne to lead the session as an “absolute tiger”, adding that members would “go pretty hard” on Gordon Brothers.

items.body:
Employee-owned sustainable fashion retailer Lucy & Yak is relocating its Nottingham store to a new site at 29 Bridlesmith Gate as it continues to invest in its UK retail estate.
The move follows strong customer demand since the brand entered Nottingham in 2023 and will place Lucy & Yak in one of the city’s best-known retail destinations, alongside a mix of established national brands and independent operators and is hot on the heels of the brand investing in a larger premises in Manchester earlier this year.
The new Nottingham store will continue to showcase the brand’s full collection alongside its Re:Yak offering, which gives customers access to repaired, pre-loved and recirculated garments.
The relocation forms part of Lucy & Yak’s broader retail strategy focused on community-led stores and circular fashion initiatives. Since launching Re:Yak three years ago, the retailer says more than 50,000 garments have been resold, repaired or recycled through the programme.
The Nottingham move follows a period of continued investment in physical retail and community activations, including the brand’s first circular fashion fair which was held last month in nearby Sheffield.
Lisa Wright, store manager, said: “Our Nottingham community has grown significantly since we first opened in the city and we’re excited to welcome customers into our new Bridlesmith Gate location. The move allows us to strengthen our presence in Nottingham while continuing to offer the colourful, inclusive shopping experience our customers know and love.”
Lydia Coley, managing director at Lucy & Yak, commented: “2026 has been quite a year for us and this move further cements our intentions to find the very best locations for our stores and loyal customers. We are fully committed to bringing colour and joy to the people of Nottingham and can’t wait to welcome everyone into our new home in the city.”
To launch the new store, Lucy & Yak will host a community-focused opening weekend featuring local artist Kim T, exclusive customer experiences, customisation workshops and promotional activity designed to celebrate both creativity and circular fashion.
Founded in Yorkshire in 2017, Lucy & Yak operates 17 stores across the UK and is known for its colourful, size-inclusive collections produced using organic and recycled materials. The business is employee-owned and continues to expand its circular retail initiatives through Re:Yak and Repairs for Life.

items.body:
Glengoyne has released its 2013 Vintage Pedro Ximénez Cask Edition, a limited batch of 9,000 bottles at 47.7% ABV and the ultimate festive dram. It launches on 11th November 2026 at an RRP of £70 and is available across selected international markets, from UK specialist retailers, and from the Glengoyne Distillery Shop and Glengoyne.com.
Vintage releases are rare for Glengoyne, and the few that exist are historic bottlings. A vintage means every cask in the release was distilled in the same year, and for this edition that year is 2013.
The recipe is made up of classic Glengoyne casks, first fill sherry and refill sherry, enhanced with fully matured first fill Pedro Ximénez casks. Glengoyne’s slow, unhurried distillation creates an open, fruity new make spirit that lets the influence of the wood shine through and, like all Glengoyne releases, it is of natural colour, drawn from time and wood alone.
The Pedro Ximénez casks give the whisky a distinctly Christmas character, with generous sweetness and depth, layers of festive fruit, warming spice and indulgent treacle toffee. Leather, freshly pressed apple juice, clove-studded oranges and milk chocolate open on the nose, followed by a rich palate of festive fruits, cranberry sauce, cinnamon and lightly stewed strawberry, and a long finish of warming spice, chocolate, treacle toffee and raisins.
It is a whisky made for the festive season, whether poured by the fire on a cold December evening, shared after Christmas dinner or wrapped and placed under the tree for the whisky lover in the family.

items.title: Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England
items.summary: Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding. Continue reading...
items.body:
Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding.
Tactics will include the expanded use of criminal behaviour orders – where repeat offenders are banned from high streets and town centres – GPS tagging and intensive supervision courts, where perpetrators must attend regular judicial hearings.
Those who do not comply or breach conditions will face imprisonment in the most serious cases, and foreign offenders could face deportation.
Mahmood said the government wanted to target people “who are causing so much harm to our communities”. She said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.”
The government said it wanted to replicate the success of Operation Kelleher, a targeted crackdown on 10 shoplifters in Bromley in 2025 that reduced recorded retail crime in the area by 70%, according to Metropolitan police data.
The number of shoplifting offences recorded by police in England and Wales rose to the highest on record in 2024, surpassing half a million offences. Last year there was a 2% decline.
The Metropolitan police said 104 repeat offenders were responsible for more than 5,300 shoplifting crimes over the past two years.
Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s, said retail crime was a “national emergency which requires a national response”. He said: “The number of incidents of theft, abuse, aggression and violence happening in stores right across the country has an unacceptable impact every single day.
“We now need to see more arrests and prosecutions of those who target UK retailers without fear of consequences and we look forward to working closely with authorities as these measures are put into action.”
Former shoplifters have spoken about how drug addiction and mental health problems are one of the main drivers of this type of crime, and charities have called for more funding for support services.
The government said the police crackdown would also be tough on the causes of crime by tackling drug and alcohol addiction “to break the cycle”.
Revolving Doors, a charity that helps to rehabilitate repeat offenders, said the scheme was a chance to “follow the evidence on what works, combining focused enforcement with sustained support to address the addiction, mental ill health and homelessness that can drive repeat offending. Success should mean fewer repeat offences and safer communities, alongside more people able to recover, contribute and realise their potential.”
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said dealing with the small group of repeat offenders responsible for a disproportionate amount of crime was crucial. “Combining robust enforcement with targeted support to tackle the root causes could make a real difference to our high streets and communities,” she said.

items.title: Why last mile should be top of mind for retailers this peak season
items.summary: Stores are handling collections, returns and courier pick-ups alongside their everyday trade. Modern Expo UK managing director Vasyl Matviiuk and client solutions and partnerships manager Sultana Kadir explain where lockers could ease the workload, and why retailers should think carefully about how much technology they need… An online order doesn’t stop creating work when it...
items.body:
Stores are handling collections, returns and courier pick-ups alongside their everyday trade. Modern Expo UK managing director Vasyl Matviiuk and client solutions and partnerships manager Sultana Kadir explain where lockers could ease the workload, and why retailers should think carefully about how much technology they need…
An online order doesn’t stop creating work when it reaches the store. Someone still has to find it, check it and hand it over, often while another customer waits to pay. Add returns and couriers collecting food orders, and staff have to divide their attention between shoppers in front of them and those whose purchases began elsewhere.
That pressure comes as retailers face tighter staffing budgets. Research from Pricer in 2025 found that 50 per cent of UK shoppers say reduced in-store staffing is negatively affecting their shopping experience, while 36 per cent of UK retailers face greater pressure to reduce labour hours or improve staff productivity due to rising wages.
It’s this pressure that Modern Expo is looking to ease with its next UK locker rollout. Following a successful proof of concept with a leading UK retailer, the company is preparing to introduce parcel lockers that allow on-demand couriers to collect orders without queuing at the till.
Couriers working through platforms such as Uber Eats, Deliveroo and Just Eat will be able to pick up in seconds, says UK managing director Vasyl Matviiuk. “That gets food to customers faster and frees store staff to serve shoppers.”
The project extends a UK locker business that has now passed 2,500 installations with Royal Mail, according to Matviiuk. Staff will still need to prepare orders and place them in compartments, but each collection will no longer require a separate handover at the counter.
Peak pressure extends into January
Matviiuk identifies capacity, cost to serve and returns as the three main pressures facing retailers this golden quarter. Rising labour and operating costs leave less room for time-consuming processes, while failed deliveries and second attempts further reduce order margins.
“The golden quarter doesn’t end in December; it ends when the returns wave clears in January,” he says.
That makes returns part of the peak-season planning challenge. Customers expect a straightforward way to hand purchases back, but stores need the space and processes to accommodate them alongside normal trade. For retailers assessing lockers, the question is broader than how many Christmas collections they can handle, it’s which services an installation could support throughout the year.
There’s also a potential sales benefit. Collection gives customers another reason to visit, creating an opportunity to sell something alongside the order they have already placed.
According to InPost UK’s 2025 research, 74 per cent of locker users visit a nearby convenience store before or after collecting a parcel, one in three spend up to £15 during their visit, and 52 per cent say having a locker nearby makes them more likely to return to the store.
“A locker is where an online order becomes a physical visit,” says Sultana Kadir, Modern Expo’s client solutions and partnerships manager.
Location is central to that opportunity. A collection point that fits into an existing shopping trip can offer convenience while bringing customers within reach of the store.
Making room for shared infrastructure
Kadir believes habit and access remain the UK’s main challenges in building locker use. She points to Poland and the Nordics as markets where collection is more established, and expects UK networks to become increasingly embedded in places people already visit.
“The next step for the UK is moving from separate, carrier-branded networks to shared infrastructure at locations people already visit, above all retail sites,” she says.
That’s her forecast for the market, but it raises a practical question for retailers considering an installation. That question is, how many different needs could it serve? A facility accommodating several carriers, customer returns and courier collections would have a different role from one restricted to a single delivery service.
With floor space at a premium during peak trading, that distinction matters. Retailers need to consider both the demand for each service and how it would fit into the store’s operation.
Choosing the technology the service needs
The same scrutiny should apply to the equipment itself. Modern Expo has exhibited lockers that keep perishables cold and food hot, but Matviiuk doesn’t argue that every food collection operation needs temperature control.
He sees a role for it where orders remain in compartments for hours. For the on-demand model the company is developing, however, he favours ambient lockers, putting the average wait for courier collection at 10 to 15 minutes.
Over that period, he argues, temperature control adds cost and complexity without changing the customer outcome. The appropriate specification will depend on the food involved and its handling requirements, making the collection process an important part of any purchasing decision.
Ambient equipment, he says, uses less energy, costs less to buy and run, and is easier to introduce across a large estate.
“Our job is to match the solution to the use case, not to over-engineer it,” adds Kadir.
Those decisions will become more significant if, as Matviiuk expects, retailers continue directing more fulfilment through their existing stores in 2027. He anticipates greater demand for automation, more shared last-mile infrastructure and closer scrutiny of floor space and energy use.
So, the investment case will rest on how well those installations perform beyond an individual trial. That includes whether they reduce the cost of handling orders, make collections more convenient and support additional store visits.
Peak season offers an immediate test, but if lockers can keep collections moving through December and help stores manage returns in January, they will have a stronger claim on the space they occupy.

items.body:
New research from American Express reveals Northern Ireland as the UK’s rewards hotspot, with loyalty programme members saving an estimated £158.40 on average over the past 12 months through rewards schemes across supermarkets and high street retailers, food and drink, travel, credit cards and third-party cashback sites.
Northern Irish consumers are making their rewards work harder than anywhere else in the UK saving more despite belonging to the fewest number of reward programmes, at eight on average compared to the national average of 12. London, where consumers are signed up to 17 loyalty schemes each – the most of anywhere in the UK – was close behind when it comes to reward programme savings, followed by Yorkshire and Humberside in third place (signed up to 12 schemes).
American Express UK Rewards League Table
Collectively, UK-based loyalty scheme members saved an estimated £4.43bn by redeeming rewards over the past year. Across each region, members are maximising the value of their everyday spending by redeeming rewards, with average savings exceeding £100 over the past 12 months:

|  |  | UK average | £132.30 | 
Caroline Bouvet, Vice President of Products and Partnerships at American Express, said: “Rewards have become much more than an occasional perk – they are now a way for consumers to get more value from their everyday spending. While consumers’ approach to rewards varies by region, it is clear they are using rewards to get more value from the money they’re already spending, whether that’s helping to reduce the cost of the weekly shop or saving towards a holiday.
“At American Express, we also understand how the value of membership extends beyond rewards. Travel and lifestyle benefits, and access to experiences, for instance, all play an important role in giving Cardmembers valuable ways to get more from their membership.”
How rewards habits differ across Britain
Around three-quarters (74%) of programme members feel they are making the most of their rewards, but the findings reveal that approaches to maximising value vary from region to region. While consumers from some regions have made rewards a routine, others use them to pay for one-off treats or unexpected costs:
· South Westerners have the biggest appetite for rewards: They are the most likely to belong to a loyalty scheme (96%, versus the UK average of 90%)
· Londoners make rewards routine: More than half (52%) say that earning and redeeming is embedded in their daily lives
· Londoners make their spending count: Members earn rewards on 38% of their everyday spending – more than anywhere in the UK
· Patience pays off in Yorkshire and Humberside: Consumers wait until there is something they specifically want or need before redeeming (34%, versus 27% on average), with only 18% saying they redeem rewards whenever they can
· North Westerners turn loyalty into personal rewards: Programme members in the region are the most likely to use rewards to treat themselves (46%, versus 38% on average across the UK)
Rewards unlock more than everyday value
Beyond the rewards they earn and redeem, three in five (59%) UK rewards programme members also receive additional perks and benefits through their programmes, such as travel upgrades, access to exclusive events, airport lounges or members-only areas, with attitudes towards these extras varying by region.
Of those receiving these additional benefits and perks, those in London, the West Midlands and the North West are the most likely to agree that additional perks and benefits make reward programmes more valuable (46%, 42% and 41% versus 35% nationally). Meanwhile those in London (40%) and Yorkshire and Humberside (37%) are among those most likely to say these benefits give them access to experiences they would not usually have.
The American Express Rewards Report 2026 explores how the UK’s rewards landscape is evolving, from how consumers earn and redeem rewards to the role they now play in everyday financial decision-making.

items.body:
OBDeleven, the connected car diagnostics and customisation platform for everyday drivers, is now available in 180 Halfords stores across the UK and Ireland, as well as on halfords.com. It is the first app-based car diagnostic tool stocked by the retailer, and the Lithuanian company’s most significant step yet into mainstream UK retail.
The pocket-sized device plugs into a car’s OBD2 port and connects to the OBDeleven app on iOS and Android, so drivers can see what is behind a warning light, run maintenance tasks and personalise their car from their phone. The rollout covers 140 stores in England, 15 in Scotland, 10 in Wales, 7 in Northern Ireland and 8 in Ireland. Strong online sales of OBDeleven prompted Halfords to bring the range into its physical stores.
OBDeleven’s UK data shows how drivers already use it. In the last 12 months, 207,498 UK vehicles connected to OBDeleven, and 85% of them ran at least one diagnostic scan. Together they ran 1.2 million scans, almost six per car a year. The average car connected to OBDeleven in the UK is ten years old, and the three most-used One-Click Apps are all maintenance tasks: oil service reset (607,255 uses), inspection reminder reset (597,598) and brake pad replacement (577,244).
“OBDeleven has already proved popular with our online customers, so bringing it into our physical stores was a natural next step. It helps drivers understand what’s behind a warning light, keep on top of servicing and personalise their car from their phone, which is exactly the kind of confidence we want to give every Halfords customer. We’re proud to be the first UK retailer to stock the OBDeleven range in store,” said Lee Mountain, commercial director at Halfords.
“Dealer-level diagnostics used to be something you either paid a garage for or picked up as a hobby. Seeing OBDeleven on the shelf at Halfords shows that’s no longer the case,” said Dainius Sapežinskas, CEO of OBDeleven. “Our UK drivers are already using it for the basics: resetting the oil service light, clearing an inspection reminder, logging new brake pads. Halfords is where British drivers go to look after their cars, so it’s the natural place to meet the ones who haven’t found us yet.”
Founded in 2014 in a Lithuanian garage and bootstrapped ever since, OBDeleven started out as a tool for car enthusiasts and has since broadened its audience to everyday drivers. It is now connected to more than 6 million cars in 60+ countries.

The new Ford E-Transits will all be on the road by mid-November as the firm gears up for the Black Friday and Christmas period, critical to business […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
The UK’s leading premium parcel delivery company DPD is set to deploy a further 381 electric vans as part of its plan for an expected record Peak period.
The new Ford E-Transits will all be on the road by mid-November as the firm gears up for the Black Friday and Christmas period, critical to business and residential customers alike.
The new 3.5t equivalent Ford E-Transits offer maximum payload and an enhanced range making them ideal for a wide range of DPD delivery routes the length and breadth of the country. DPD is no stranger to the Ford E-Transit having first deployed them back in early 2022.
The order follows hot on the heels of the delivery of 341 new Mercedes-Benz eSprinter vans in September as the firm continues to invest in more sustainable fleet solutions.
The investment is part of DPD’s ongoing aim to be the UK’s leader in sustainable delivery. In 2025 DPD delivered over 85 million parcels on electric vehicles including a predominantly diesel-free final mile service within the North and South Circular in London.
Olly Craughan, DPD’s head of sustainability and social purpose, commented, “Ford is a strong partner for DPD, and we already operate a significant number of E-Transits. They have performed well for us over the last four years, while the TrustFord mobile service network also played a big part in us choosing Ford again. The enhanced range means we can now get more of these larger electric vans out on our longer routes, making a bigger difference in terms of reducing emissions.
“This is set to be our biggest peak yet, so it is great to be able to say to customers that we will have more electric vans delivering on the road than ever before. We know this is a key issue for many shippers, large and small and we are delighted to be delivering more of their parcels on electric vehicles.”
Details on all of DPD’s sustainability initiatives can be found on its dedicated website.

items.title: National Lottery Christmas campaign launched to help drive retail footfall
items.summary: National Lottery retailers across the UK are set to benefit from Allwyn UK's first brand-led Christmas campaign for The National Lottery. Running for 10 weeks from 7 November through to early January, ‘This Christmas It Could Be You’ is backed by an integrated programme spanning… This story continues at National Lottery Christmas campaign launched to help drive retail footfall Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Running for 10 weeks from 7 November through to early January, ‘This Christmas It Could Be You’ is backed by an integrated programme spanning TV, out-of-home, cinema, digital, retail and creator partnerships, designed to drive player engagement, increase store visits and support sales throughout the busy Christmas trading period.
The campaign is led by a new hero TV ad featuring the voice of The National Lottery’s ambassador-in-chief, Claudia Winkleman, delivering the closing sign-off: “Amazing Things Happen When You Believe. This Christmas It Could Be You.”
Christmas is traditionally one of the most important trading periods of the year for National Lottery retailers, and this year’s activity has been designed to drive awareness of the full National Lottery portfolio, including Lotto, EuroMillions and Scratchcards.
Approximately 41,000 National Lottery retail outlets will be supported by enhanced festive point-of-sale materials, standout displays and in-store media, helping retailers capture shoppers’ attention and maximise sales opportunities during the busy Christmas season.
The National Lottery’s festive Scratchcard range is expected to be a key feature of this year’s Christmas offering, with research showing that 75% of players are likely to gift Scratchcards during the festive season.
Leading the range is the premium £10 ‘When It’s Gold Outside’ Scratchcard, which offers players 37 chances to win and four top prizes of £4m.
Alongside it is a range of festive games across multiple price points, including ‘Christmas Countdown’, ‘Frosty Fortunes’, ‘Tinsel Trail’, ‘Feastive Fortunes’ and ‘Just to Say’, helping retailers meet demand for stocking fillers, Christmas card inserts and festive gifts, while earning 6% commission on every Scratchcard sale.
Retailers can also look forward to a packed schedule of major Lotto and EuroMillions events throughout the festive period. Following the launch of Lotto’s new two-round format earlier this year, two £12m Lotto Must Be Won draws are scheduled for 21 November and 23 December. Meanwhile, a EuroMillions Super Jackpot draw estimated at £109m is due to take place on 4 December, followed by two 10 UK Millionaire events on Christmas Day and 29 December.
Independent retailers also have the chance to share in the festive celebrations through Allwyn’s retailer Advent Calendar.
Running from 1 to 25 December on the TNL Partners Hub, the calendar offers more than 5,000 prizes worth a combined £50,000.
Retailers can win daily prizes of up to £250, while each window opened also earns an entry into a Festive Finale draw featuring 10 prizes of £1,000.
To promote responsible play during the festive season, Allwyn is also rolling out a Christmas Gift Responsibly programme across National Lottery channels.
Activity includes a dedicated section on The National Lottery Responsible Play page, retailer communications, updated messaging on in-store digital screens, bespoke responsible gifting creative across social media channels, and the inclusion of the ’18+ Gift Responsibly’ mark across all gifting-related festive advertising, alongside responsible play messaging within seasonal Scratchcard advertising.
The initiative reinforces the message that National Lottery products can only be bought, gifted, received and played by people aged 18 or over, while providing practical guidance for players and retailers during the busy Christmas period.
Bridget Lea, managing director – retail at Allwyn, said: “Christmas is such an important time of year for our retail partners. We know that strong awareness and excitement can make a real difference during the festive trading period.
“This year, we’re backing The National Lottery with a major festive marketing campaign designed to drive excitement across the full portfolio of games and make it part of the UK’s Christmas celebrations.
“From our heartwarming new Christmas advert and nationwide media campaign to in-store activity, a fantastic range of festive Scratchcards and major Lotto and EuroMillions events, everything has been designed to capture people’s imagination and inspire them to believe that amazing things can happen.
“Together, these activities will help retailers make the most of the festive trading period, all the while bringing the magic of The National Lottery to communities across the UK through Good Cause funding.”

items.title: Black Friday 2026: food and drink emerge as new opportunities for brands, retailers and hospitality outlets
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. More than three-quarters (77%) of UK shoppers plan to take part in Black Friday this year, as ongoing cost-of-living pressures put value firmly in focus ahead of Christmas, according to new research from retail and shopper marketing agency Savvy. The findings reveal how Black Friday is evolving beyond its traditional electricals and fashion heartland, presenting […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
More than three-quarters (77%) of UK shoppers plan to take part in Black Friday this year, as ongoing cost-of-living pressures put value firmly in focus ahead of Christmas, according to new research from retail and shopper marketing agency Savvy.
The findings reveal how Black Friday is evolving beyond its traditional electricals and fashion heartland, presenting growing opportunities for food and drink brands, supermarkets and hospitality operators.
Alastair Lockhart, insight director at Savvy, commented: “Despite some concerns about the credibility of discounts, shoppers continue to see significant value in the event. Almost three-quarters of shoppers believe Black Friday offers the best deals of the year, while 72% say discounts allowed them to buy products they wouldn’t normally be able to afford. With the cost of living very much front of mind, the Black Friday sales period has become an essential part of many shoppers’ festive buying plans.”
The event is increasingly important for Christmas shopping, with 84% agreeing that Black Friday was a good time to buy gifts. Six in 10 (60%) shoppers have specifically saved money to spend during Black Friday, underlining the extent to which the occasion has become a planned part of household spending.
Black Friday now a festive shopping fixture, not just a day
While Black Friday officially falls on 27 November this year, shoppers increasingly see it as an extended sales period rather than a single-day event. Savvy’s research found that 42% of shoppers expect to shop Black Friday deals in the weeks leading up to the event and 40% plan to shop on Black Friday itself. Meanwhile, 19% expect to make purchases in the days and weeks that follow.
“As retailers continue to extend their promotional activity, Black Friday has become a longer window of opportunity to engage shoppers. For brands and retailers, this has created more opportunities to reach shoppers at different stages of their purchasing journey, from early deal research through to later Christmas purchases. The challenge, of course, is balancing the need to stimulate demand with protecting margins during this crucial trading period,” added Lockhart.
Physical stores remain relevant, with 42% of shoppers expected to shop Black Friday deals in-store; 52% planned to shop online.
Social commerce has also started to establish a role in the event. One in 10 shoppers expected to buy through social media platforms such as TikTok Shop, rising to 22% among households with children.
Shoppers want value, but remain sceptical about deals
While shoppers recognised the benefits of Black Friday, there was tension between the appeal of discounts and concerns about the authenticity of some. Three-quarters (76%) of shoppers said they often questioned whether Black Friday discounts were as good as they seemed, while 80% believed the event encouraged people to buy things they didn’t need.
Technology also placed a growing role. Over half (55%) of shoppers said they would use AI to help find the best deals, highlighting growing interest in tools that could compare prices rapidly and identify genuine value.
However, Black Friday is not simply about finding familiar products at lower prices. More than two-thirds (68%) of shoppers agreed that the event helped them to discover new brands.
Fashion and electricals lead, but food and drink show significant potential
Clothing and footwear topped the list of planned Black Friday purchases, selected by 37% of shoppers, closely followed by electricals and gadgets at 34%. However, food was not far behind, with 29% expecting to purchase food products during the occasion. Health and beauty products (26%), homeware (25%) and toys and games (23%) were also popular categories. One in five shoppers planned to buy books, music, films or video games (20%), while alcoholic drinks and soft drinks were each selected by 19%.
Black Friday presents growth opportunities
Savvy’s research suggested that shopper appetite for food and drink promotions is considerably greater than current purchasing intentions might have indicated.
More than eight in 10 shoppers (82%) believed supermarkets should offer Black Friday discounts on groceries, while 83% would have liked their favourite food and drink brands to participate in the occasion.
The opportunity extended across both everyday essentials and seasonal purchases. Over three-quarters (76%) said they would use Black Friday deals to stock up on everyday food and drink products, while 79% would use discounts to buy food and drink for Christmas.
There is also an opportunity to encourage shoppers to trade up. Three-quarters (76%) said Black Friday discounts would encourage them to buy premium food and drink products they wouldn’t normally purchase, while 73% saw the occasion as a good opportunity to try new food and drink brands.
Lockhart concluded: “Black Friday presents a particularly interesting opportunity for food and drink brands. With the right categories and offers, retailers can encourage shoppers to trade up, try new products and make additional purchases during the festive period. The opportunity is to generate incremental sales, rather than simply bring forward purchases at a lower margin – a challenge that can be particularly acute in categories such as electricals and fashion.”
Black Friday extends into hospitality and foodservice
The opportunity for food and drink is not limited to supermarket shelves. Black Friday is also highly relevant to restaurants, cafés, pubs and takeaway businesses.
More than one in four shoppers (27%) expected to order a takeaway or food delivery using a Black Friday deal, while 21% planned to eat at a restaurant offering a promotion. One in five (20%) expected to visit a café or coffee shop offering a deal, with 17% planning to visit a pub or bar participating in the occasion.
Almost three-quarters (72%) agreed they would be more likely to visit a restaurant, pub or bar if it offered Black Friday deals.
These findings highlight an opportunity for hospitality businesses to use Black Friday to stimulate visits and orders, particularly as consumers balance the desire to enjoy themselves with the need to manage spending.
For operators, promotions that offer a clear sense of value, whether through set menus, bundled offers or incentives to visit, could provide an effective way to attract customers during the extended Black Friday period.
